steps.title: D1 - T1 — Module boundary: a shared state object, not scattered module lets
steps.narration: app.js had ~15 top-level `var`s that every function could read AND write. Splitting into modules, I could have made each one its own exported `let` — but an ES module import binding is read-only in the importing module: `import { allEvidence } from './state.js'; allEvidence = x` throws, because only the module that declared a binding may reassign it. Almost every one of these values gets reassigned (not just read) from a DIFFERENT module than the one that first sets it — e.g. evidence.js does `state.allEvidence = data` after a fetch that actually happens in dataLoading.js. So instead of exported `let`s plus a setter function per variable, I put them all as properties on one exported `state` object: mutating a property of an imported object is fine, only rebinding the imported name itself is restricted. Same values, same semantics as the old globals — just relocated so the read/write rule is explicit instead of implicit.

steps.title: D1 - T2 — Loading the entry point as a module script
steps.narration: A classic `<script src="app.js">` executes eagerly, in the global scope, in non-strict mode, and has no import/export syntax available — every function and var in app.js became a `window` property, which is exactly why 6-7 of app.js's functions had to leak onto `window` again after the split, just to satisfy inline onclick/onchange HTML attributes that only ever run in global scope. `<script type="module">` instead: runs in strict mode automatically, gets its own module-level scope (so `js/main.js`'s top-level names don't become globals), is deferred by default (doesn't block parsing, runs after the DOM is parsed), and only this tag can use `import`/`export` at all — without it, every `import` statement in js/main.js and everything it pulls in would be a syntax error. It also only works over HTTP, not `file://` — same CORS-style same-origin restriction that already forced this app to be served via `python -m http.server` for `fetch()` to work.
steps.before: <script src="app.js"></script>
steps.after: <script type="module" src="js/main.js"></script>

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — classic <script> vs <script type="module">
steps.narration: Two behavioral differences that actually mattered here: (1) module scripts execute after the DOM is parsed, in document order, like `defer` — a classic `<script src="app.js">` at the end of body instead ran immediately, blocking parsing at that point. (2) A module's top-level declarations are scoped to that module, not attached to `window` — classic-script top-level `var`/function declarations do leak onto `window`. That's exactly why `js/main.js` has to explicitly do `window.navigateTo = navigateTo` and five more like it: the HTML's inline `onclick="navigateTo(...)"` attributes always execute in global scope, so functions the HTML calls by name have to be deliberately re-attached to `window` now that they're module-private by default.

steps.title: D1 - Q2 — reading/writing allEvidence across modules
steps.narration: Before the refactor, `allEvidence` was a bare global `var` — any code in `app.js` read or wrote it by name directly. After the split, a different module has to `import { state } from "./state.js"` (see js/views/evidence.js:10) and go through `state.allEvidence` — property reads/writes on the imported object are fine (e.g. js/dataLoading.js:65's `state.allEvidence = data;`), but you can never rebind the imported `state` name itself, and a module that never imported it at all can't reference `allEvidence` bare. Forget the import and reference `allEvidence` directly in a module: `ReferenceError: allEvidence is not defined`. That error is actually useful — modules are strict mode and have no implicit-global fallback, so the failure is loud and immediate, pointing exactly at the missing import, rather than the old classic-script failure mode of silently creating a stray global or reading stale data with no error at all.

steps.title: D1 - Q3 (1/2) — named export: js/lookup.js
steps.narration: A named export (js/lookup.js: `findEvidenceById`, `findPersonById`, `findLocationById`, and four more not shown here) exports several specifically-named, equally-weighted bindings — there's no single 'main' thing lookup.js provides, so each helper gets its own named export, imported elsewhere as `import { findEvidenceById, ... } from "../lookup.js"`. Contrast with js/dataLoading.js:97's default export (next slide) — chose default there specifically because `loadAllData` really is the one and only public entry point of that module, whereas lookup.js has seven small, independent utilities and no such single 'main' export to prefer.

steps.title: D1 - Q3 (2/2) — default export: js/dataLoading.js
steps.narration: A default export is for a module with exactly one thing external code needs. js/dataLoading.js's `loadCorePeopleAndLocations`, `loadEvidenceData`, `loadTimelineData`, `showLoadingOverlay`, and `hideLoadingStep` all stay unexported — only `loadAllData` is ever called from outside the module (js/main.js:16: `import loadAllData from "./dataLoading.js"` — no braces, unlike a named import). Contrast with the previous slide's js/lookup.js, where seven independent, equally-weighted helpers each need their own named export instead.

steps.title: D1 - Q4 — why file:// breaks both modules and fetch()
steps.narration: Same underlying cause, two different enforcement points. Module scripts resolve each `import` as its own network-style request under CORS/same-origin rules — under `file://` there's no real origin to satisfy that, so the browser refuses to load the module graph at all (a console error like 'Cross origin requests are only supported for HTTP' before any of this code even runs). The app's own `fetch()` calls for `data/*.json` in dataLoading.js hit the identical restriction for the identical reason — no valid origin under `file://`. So: same root cause (no HTTP origin under `file://`), just tripped by two separate browser mechanisms — module resolution vs. runtime `fetch()`.

steps.title: D2 - T1 (1/2) — Reproducing the bug: baseline state before touching Evidence sort
steps.narration: Repro setup: I added a private note to E01 (“Morning calibration failure report”) and a private note to E02 (“Robot diagnostic log”) from the Evidence detail view, then opened Workspace. The Personal Notes list shows them in id order — E01 first, then E02 — and the hypothesis form's “Selected supporting evidence” picker below it lists all 18 items E01…E18 in that same original load order. Nothing here touches the Evidence catalogue's own sort control yet — this is just the honest baseline I compare against next.

steps.title: D2 - T1 (2/2) — Reproducing the bug: sorting the Evidence catalogue
steps.narration: From Workspace I navigate to Evidence and change only the “Sort evidence” dropdown to “Title (Z–A)” — I don't touch bookmarks, notes, or the hypothesis form at all. That fires handleSortChange() in views/evidence.js, which calls state.filteredEvidence.sort(...). Going straight back to Workspace afterward (no reload), the Personal Notes list now reads E02 then E01 — flipped — and the hypothesis evidence picker is now in full title-descending order (E18, E02, E09, E14…). A control on a completely different view silently reordered data two other views depend on. This reproduces every single time, from a fresh page load, with no timing sensitivity.

steps.title: D2 - T2 — Root cause: filteredEvidence aliased allEvidence instead of copying it
steps.narration: js/dataLoading.js's loadEvidenceData did `state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence;` — that's an assignment of the array reference, not a copy, so allEvidence and filteredEvidence were literally the same array object in memory. state.allEvidence is meant to be the canonical, stable list every other view relies on (Dashboard, Workspace's notes list, the hypothesis picker); state.filteredEvidence is meant to be a disposable, re-derived “current view” that the Evidence catalogue filters and sorts. Because they were the same object, handleSortChange()'s in-place `state.filteredEvidence.sort(...)` reordered allEvidence too. Normally getFilteredEvidence() (evidence.js) would break that alias the first time the Evidence list actually renders — it does `state.filteredEvidence = results` with a freshly built array. But a separate, pre-existing bug (state.evidenceViewLoading is initialized true in state.js and is never set back to false anywhere in the codebase — confirmed by grepping the whole repo) means renderEvidenceList() always takes its early-return branch and getFilteredEvidence() never runs, so in the current build that alias is never broken and the corruption is permanent, not just a narrow race. I confirmed this directly in the console (`(await import('/js/state.js')).state.allEvidence === state.filteredEvidence` → true before the fix) rather than just inferring it from the symptom. The fix: copy on load with `.slice()`, so filteredEvidence is independent from the very first assignment — exactly matching what getFilteredEvidence() already does on every real render, just applied at load time too. (The evidenceViewLoading stuck-flag bug itself is real but separate — noted for a later demo, not fixed here.)

steps.title: D2 - T3 — Verifying the fix: Workspace order now stays stable, nearby features untouched
steps.narration: I repeated the exact repro after the fix: seed the same two notes, note the Workspace baseline (E01, E02, full E01…E18 picker order), go sort the Evidence catalogue every which way (title asc/desc, date asc/desc), then come straight back to Workspace — the Personal Notes list and the hypothesis evidence picker never move now, confirmed via `state.allEvidence === state.filteredEvidence` reading false right after load. I also spot-checked the features nearest to this code: the Evidence detail panel (notes, status, relevance editing) still works exactly as before — opened via Timeline's quick-view “Open full evidence” button, since the catalogue's own card list has its own separate stuck-loading bug unrelated to this fix, left untouched for a later demo — and the Dashboard's evidence/people/location counts and the People view's per-person evidence counts, which don't depend on array order at all, were unaffected either way.

steps.title: D2 - Q1 — reference vs. copy, and how aliasing caused this bug
steps.narration: A *copy* is an independent array/object in memory holding the same current contents — changing one afterward doesn't touch the other. A *reference* is just another variable pointing at the SAME object — mutating through either name changes the one underlying object both point at, and `===` between them is true. Before the fix, `state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence;` assigned the reference, not the contents, so `state.allEvidence === state.filteredEvidence` was true (I re-confirmed live: false on the current fixed build, and it was true on the pre-fix commit bf8e25d). Because handleSortChange() in js/views/evidence.js calls `.sort()` directly on state.filteredEvidence, and Array.prototype.sort mutates its array in place and returns that same reference rather than a new array, sorting 'the catalogue's view' and sorting 'the canonical list' were literally the same operation on the same object — there was only one array to sort. The fix, `state.allEvidence.slice()`, makes a shallow copy: a new, independent array holding references to the same evidence item objects. That's the right depth of copy — I verified live that `state.allEvidence[0] === state.filteredEvidence[0]` is still true post-fix, which is correct and intentional: editing an item's status/relevance/note in the detail view is supposed to stay visible from both arrays. Only the arrays' element ORDER needed to become independent, not the item objects themselves.

steps.title: D2 - Q2 — the exact trigger sequence, and could static reading have caught it
steps.narration:
Exact trigger, reproduced live: load the app fresh, add a note to E01 and to E02 via the Evidence detail panel, open Workspace — Notes list reads in the canonical load order (E01, E02). Go to Evidence and change ONLY the 'Sort evidence' dropdown to 'Title (Z–A)' — nothing else touched. That fires handleSortChange() (js/views/evidence.js), which runs state.filteredEvidence.sort(...) in place. At that exact moment, because state.filteredEvidence and state.allEvidence were still the same array object (the aliasing bug), the in-place sort reordered both simultaneously. Navigate back to Workspace without reloading — the Notes list and the hypothesis evidence picker are now in title-descending order, even though neither view's own code ever touched sorting.

Could reading top-to-bottom, without running it, have found this? Only partially, and it's not a fair 'obvious at a glance' bug. `state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence;`, read in isolation inside loadEvidenceData, looks like ordinary initialization — nothing on that single line signals danger unless you're already actively watching for reference-aliasing. The bug only becomes visible once you additionally know two more facts that live in a DIFFERENT file: that Array.prototype.sort() mutates in place rather than returning a new array (unlike, say, .map() or .filter()), and that handleSortChange() calls that mutating sort directly on state.filteredEvidence. Neither fact is visible from dataLoading.js alone — you'd have to trace every consumer of state.filteredEvidence across the codebase, recognize handleSortChange as one of them, and separately recall .sort()'s in-place semantics, to connect it back to the aliasing assignment three files away. That's a multi-file, semantics-dependent trace, not a pattern-match on one suspicious line — which is exactly why I found this by running the app and noticing the symptom (Workspace order changing after an Evidence-only action), not by reading the source first.

steps.title: D3 - T1 (1/2) — Reproducing the bug: confirming the data itself loaded fine
steps.narration: Before blaming the fetch, I ruled it out: on a fresh load, the Dashboard's 'Evidence items' stat reads 18 — that number comes straight from state.allEvidence.length inside renderDashboard(), so seeing it correct is independent proof that fetch("data/evidence.json") in loadEvidenceData() succeeded and state.allEvidence was fully populated. Whatever's broken next, it isn't the fetch failing or the data never arriving.

steps.title: D3 - T1 (2/2) — Reproducing the bug: the catalogue never leaves "Loading evidence…"
steps.narration: Navigating straight to Evidence from that same load — no reload, no delay — the card list stayed permanently empty and the "Loading evidence…" placeholder never went away, even though the Dashboard (previous slide) had just proven the data had arrived. I confirmed this with Playwright, not just eyeballing it: querying #evidenceList showed zero .evidence-card elements and #evidenceLoadingIndicator without the 'hidden' class, reliably, on every fresh load — not flaky, not a timing race, just permanently stuck.

steps.title: D3 - T2 — Root cause: evidenceViewLoading is set true and never set back to false
steps.narration: renderEvidenceList() (js/views/evidence.js) gates the whole catalogue render on state.evidenceViewLoading — while true it shows the placeholder and returns immediately, before ever reaching getFilteredEvidence() or building any cards. That flag is declared `evidenceViewLoading: true` in js/state.js, clearly meant to flip false once the evidence.json fetch that's supposed to populate the catalogue resolves. I grepped the entire repo for every reference to it and found exactly three: the `true` initialization, this `if` check, and nothing else — no callback, anywhere, ever assigned it `false`. So the flag wasn't reset by a slow fetch or a race; it was never going to be reset at all, by design-gone-wrong: the person who wrote the placeholder logic never wired up the code that was supposed to clear it once loadEvidenceData()'s fetch settled. I confirmed this is the actual cause (not just a plausible-looking dead flag) live: after load, state.allEvidence.length was 18 while state.evidenceViewLoading was still true — the exact combination this hypothesis predicts.

steps.title: D3 - T3 — Fix: set evidenceViewLoading false once the fetch that promised it settles
steps.narration: The fix sets state.evidenceViewLoading = false directly inside loadEvidenceData()'s fetch chain, in both the success .then (right after the data it's waiting for has actually landed in state.allEvidence/state.filteredEvidence) and the failure .catch (the fetch has settled either way — leaving the placeholder up forever on a failed load would be just as broken). This isn't a delay or a retry papering over a symptom: it's the exact state update the async success/failure callbacks were supposed to make and never did, added at the exact point in the Promise lifecycle where it belongs — once resolved/rejected, not before. Verified live post-fix: #evidenceList now shows all 18 .evidence-card elements and #evidenceLoadingIndicator has 'hidden' set, matching the Dashboard's count from the very first repro slide.

steps.title: D3 - Q1 — the async operation, and where in its lifecycle the bug actually lived
steps.narration: The operation is fetch("data/evidence.json") in loadEvidenceData() (js/dataLoading.js) — it fetches the full 18-item evidence catalogue that this view's card list renders. The bug isn't before the fetch starts (evidenceViewLoading correctly starts true so the placeholder shows while pending) and it isn't a failure-path bug either — it's on the success path: once the Promise resolved and handed back real data, the success callback was supposed to flip evidenceViewLoading to false so renderEvidenceList() would stop early-returning the placeholder, and it just never did. I didn't guess this — I confirmed it two ways: (1) reading the code, grepping the whole repo for every reference to evidenceViewLoading and finding no write site anywhere except the true initializer; (2) reproducing live with Playwright and checking both values directly after load — state.allEvidence.length was 18 (the fetch had resolved and delivered data) while state.evidenceViewLoading was still true (the flag its resolution was supposed to update never moved). That combination — data present, flag never flipped — is only explainable by something that should have run on the Promise's success path never running, which is exactly what Demo 3 is asking for.

steps.title: D4 - T1 — Reproducing the bug: a TypeError on every nav-button click, zero UI symptom
steps.narration: With DevTools' Console tab open for the whole session (Demo 4's rule), clicking any nav button — Dashboard, Evidence, People & Locations, Timeline, Workspace — throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'getAttribute')` at js/main.js:44, every single time. But look at the page itself: the URL hash updates, the correct view renders, the clicked button gets the active state — nothing visibly broke. That's the whole point of this demo: an error is firing on every interaction and the UI gives no indication anything is wrong.

steps.title: D4 - T2 — Root cause: var in a for loop shares one binding across every closure
steps.narration: setupEventListeners() (js/main.js) loops over the 5 nav buttons and calls addEventListener("click", function() {...}) once per button, and each of those callback closures reads `navButtons[i]`. `var i` is function-scoped, not block-scoped — there is exactly ONE `i` variable for the whole loop, shared by all 5 closures, not a fresh one per iteration. By the time a user actually clicks a button — always later, after the loop has already finished all 5 iterations — `i` has already reached its final value, `navButtons.length` (5). `navButtons[5]` is `undefined`, so `.getAttribute("data-view")` throws. This is a textbook closure-over-a-shared-loop-variable bug (course Chapter 2 — Scope, Closures, and Function Forms): the closures don't capture the value of `i` at creation time, they capture the variable itself, and that variable keeps changing after each closure is created.

steps.title: D4 - T3 — Fix: let instead of var gives each closure its own binding; console now clean
steps.narration: Changing `var i` to `let i` is the whole fix — `let` in a `for` loop header creates a brand-new, independently-scoped binding of `i` for each iteration, initialized to that iteration's value, so each of the 5 click closures captures its own `i` (0 through 4) instead of all 5 sharing one final, out-of-range `i`. No other line changes: this listener was already dead weight (actual navigation runs through the separate onclick="navigateTo(...)" attribute in index.html), so the minimal, scope-correct fix is exactly right here rather than restructuring the listener. Verified live after the fix: clicking Dashboard → Evidence → People → Timeline → Workspace in sequence now logs `nav clicked: dashboard`, `nav clicked: evidence`, `nav clicked: people`, `nav clicked: timeline`, `nav clicked: workspace` — each matching the actual button clicked — with zero console errors, where before every single click produced the TypeError.

steps.title: D4 - Q1 — How I noticed it, and why "looks fine" isn't "is fine"
steps.narration: I noticed this only because DevTools' Console was open and visible for the entire session, per Demo 4's rule, not because anything on screen prompted me to look. Every nav-button click renders correctly — the crashing addEventListener block in js/main.js is dead code left over from an earlier version: real navigation runs entirely through the separate onclick="navigateTo(...)" attribute on each button in index.html, so nothing downstream ever depends on the crashing handler's result. "Nothing looks broken" only tells you the specific paths you happened to exercise, with the specific outputs something else happened to consume, behaved correctly — it says nothing about code that runs and fails but whose result nobody reads (exactly this bug), code paths nobody has clicked through yet, or other silent bugs sitting elsewhere in the app that Demo 5 is explicitly built to go find. The only way to tell "quiet because it's actually fine" apart from "quiet because nobody's watching" is to keep the console open and actually look — which is the real practice this demo is testing, not a formality.

steps.title: D5 - T1 (1/7) — Bug: loadNoteAsync's Promise logged unresolved
steps.narration: Repro: load the app fresh with the console open — no clicking required, this fires on every single page load. Expected: "First note preview: <the stored note text, or an empty string if none>". Actual: "First note preview: Promise" followed by a pending Promise object, every time. Root cause: loadNoteAsync (js/storage.js) returns `new Promise(function (resolve) { resolve(...) })` — it's async by contract, even though it resolves synchronously under the hood — but initApp (js/main.js) called it with `var firstNote = loadNoteAsync("E01");` and logged `firstNote` directly, which is the Promise object itself, not its resolved value. Fix: chain `.then()` and log the value the Promise actually resolves to. Verified live: with a note first cleared from localStorage, reload logs "First note preview: " (empty string); with `remotion_notes` seeded to `{"E01":"Test note content"}` via `localStorage.setItem`, reload logs "First note preview: Test note content" — confirming this isn't just "no longer a Promise" but the actually-correct resolved text in both the empty and populated cases.

steps.title: D5 - T1 (2/7) — Bug: timeline events show "Location: [object Object]"
steps.narration: Repro: open the Timeline view — no filtering needed, it's visible on the default unfiltered list. Expected: each event with a resolvable location shows something like "Location: L01 - Human-Robot Interaction Laboratory". Actual: every single one of the 15 events that have a resolvable location instead literally reads "Location: [object Object]" — confirmed by querying all 15 `.evidence-meta` location lines live and getting that exact string back for every one. Root cause: `findLocationById` (js/lookup.js) returns the location *object*, not a display string. renderTimeline pushed that object directly into `eventLocationNames` (`eventLocationNames.push(evtLoc || item.locationIds[el])`), then called `.join(", ")` on the array — Array.join() calls `.toString()` on non-string elements, and a plain object's default `.toString()` is the literal string "[object Object]". Fix: format the object into "id - name" before pushing, matching the exact convention evidence.js's own detail view already uses for the same kind of location list (`loc.id + " - " + loc.name`) — not inventing a new display format. Verified live: after the fix, the same 15 lines read e.g. "Location: L01 - Human-Robot Interaction Laboratory", "Location: L04 - Infrastructure Operations Room", etc.

steps.title: D5 - T1 (3/7) — Bug: unguarded JSON.parse on hand-edited localStorage crashes the app
steps.narration: Repro (the notes case, the more severe of the two): in DevTools, `localStorage.setItem('remotion_notes', '{not valid json!!!')`, then reload the page — exactly the "hand-edit localStorage... replace a value with text that isn't valid JSON" scenario this demo's own instructions call out. Expected: worst case, notes fail to load and the rest of the app works (matching how loadBookmarksFromStorage already handles this same situation one function above it). Actual: an uncaught SyntaxError from JSON.parse throws inside loadNotesFromStorage, which runs synchronously and unconditionally as literally the second line of initApp — before setupEventListeners() and loadAllData() ever run. The whole boot aborts: no event listeners attached, no data loaded, the page is stuck forever on "Loading case file…" with completely dead nav buttons. Confirmed via the exact stack trace live: "SyntaxError ... at loadNotesFromStorage (storage.js:41) at initApp (main.js:78)". A second, independent instance of the identical pattern lives in workspace.js's loadHypothesisFromStorage — corrupt `remotion_hypothesis` and every single Workspace-view render throws instead (confirmed via its own stack trace), a narrower but still real break. Fix: wrap both JSON.parse calls in try/catch, exactly mirroring the try/catch loadBookmarksFromStorage (js/storage.js, just above loadNotesFromStorage) already used correctly for the same kind of hand-editable data. Verified live: with both keys corrupted, the app now boots normally (dashboard renders, overlay hides) and Workspace renders its form fields normally too — only a console.warn appears instead of a fatal, boot-aborting exception.

steps.title: D5 - T1 (4/7) — Bug: Evidence catalogue Sort dropdown is completely non-functional (CHOSEN for live demo)
steps.narration: Repro: open Evidence, leave every filter at its default, change "Sort evidence" to any option (e.g. "Title (Z–A)"). Expected: the 18 cards reorder accordingly. Actual: nothing changes — the list stays in original E01, E02, E03… order, 100% of the time, from the very first use, not a race condition. Confirmed directly in the console: setting the dropdown's value and calling `window.handleSortChange()` still leaves the rendered card order matching `allEvidence`'s original order, not the selected sort. Root cause: `handleSortChange()` sorted `state.filteredEvidence` in place, then called `renderEvidenceList()` — which calls `getFilteredEvidence()`, and THAT function unconditionally rebuilds `state.filteredEvidence` from `state.allEvidence` in original order (filtered only) and reassigns it, discarding the sort before a single frame ever renders it. The very call that's supposed to show the sorted result is what erases it. Fix: move the sort into `getFilteredEvidence()` itself, as the last step of every filter rebuild (new private `applyCurrentSortOrder` helper), so the current sort selection survives filtering instead of being a one-render-only effect that never even lasts one render. Verified live, twice: (1) setting sort to title-desc now shows Team → Robot → Refactor Rex's... → Production → Patch Vector's... (correct Z–A order); (2) changing a filter afterward keeps that same sort order instead of resetting to unsorted — confirming the fix survives the exact interaction that most needed it. This is the bug I chose for the live class demo — no localStorage setup required, fully deterministic, single clear root cause.

steps.title: D5 - T1 (5/7) — Bug: timeline quick-view modal stacks a new click listener on every open
steps.narration: Repro: on Timeline, click "View <id>" to open the quick-view modal, close it, then click "View <id>" on a *different* event to reopen it. Expected: the modal behaves the same regardless of how many times it's been opened before. Actual: each open silently stacks one more listener on the same, reused `#quickViewModal` element (only its innerHTML gets replaced between opens, the element itself is created once and kept) — confirmed by instrumenting `window.setTimeout`: after exactly 2 opens, a single click on "Open full evidence" triggered 2 stacked calls into the setTimeout-wrapped `openEvidenceDetail` scheduling, not 1. The codebase even had a breadcrumb for this: `state.modalCloseListenerCount` was incremented and logged on every open specifically to surface the growing listener count. Root cause: `openEvidenceModal` called `modal.addEventListener("click", function (e) {...})` with a brand-new anonymous function literal every single call — addEventListener only dedupes identical function *references*, and a fresh closure is never identical to the last one, so nothing was ever dedup'd. Fix: hoist the handler to one named function (`handleModalClick`), declared once at module scope, and only call addEventListener the first time the modal element is created (the same dedupe pattern evidence.js's own card-list click handler already uses correctly) — also removes the now-pointless `modalCloseListenerCount` debug counter. Verified live: the identical setTimeout-instrumentation test after the fix returns exactly 1 call, not 2, and the modal's close/open-full behavior still works correctly.

steps.title: D5 - T1 (6/7) — Bug: hypothesis form's evidence multi-select silently forgets unsaved selections
steps.narration: Repro: on Workspace, select a couple of items in "Selected supporting evidence" (e.g. E03 and E05) and type something into "Written explanation" — don't click Save. Navigate to any other view, then back to Workspace. Expected: unsaved in-progress edits either all persist or all reset, consistently. Actual: the explanation text survives untouched, but the evidence selection is silently wiped back to nothing selected — confirmed live by reading both fields' values immediately before navigating away and again immediately after navigating back. Root cause: `renderWorkspace()` re-renders unconditionally on every visit to the Workspace view (by design, per this codebase's own comment: "workspace is cheap enough that it always re-renders"), which calls `populateHypothesisDropdowns()` every time. That function already protects the single-select suspect dropdown correctly — it captures `suspectSelect.value` before rebuilding its innerHTML and restores it after — but the multi-select evidence dropdown's innerHTML gets rebuilt from scratch with no options ever marked selected, and nothing captured its prior selection first. Fix: apply the exact same capture-before-rebuild/restore-after pattern already used for the suspect dropdown, reusing the existing `getSelectedOptions` helper (previously only used inside saveHypothesis). Verified live: select E03+E05, type an explanation, navigate Workspace → Evidence → Workspace — both the explanation text AND the E03/E05 selection now survive the round trip.

steps.title: D5 - T1 (7/7) — Bug: loading overlay budgeted for 2 steps but 3 actually run
steps.narration: This one is a latent correctness bug rather than something reliably visible on localhost (all three data files are tiny and fetch near-instantly from a local server, so the race rarely shows up to the eye) — found by reading, not by clicking, and included because the code is objectively wrong regardless of how often it's visibly triggered. Root cause: `loadAllData()` sets `state.loadingStepsRemaining = 2` and then kicks off three independent async steps — core (people/locations), evidence, and timeline — each of which is supposed to call `hideLoadingStep()` once it settles. `loadCorePeopleAndLocations` and `loadTimelineData` both do; `loadEvidenceData` never did, at all, in either its success or failure path. So the counter could reach zero — and the "Loading case file…" overlay dismiss — as soon as core and timeline settled, regardless of whether evidence.json had actually finished loading yet. On a slower connection (or Demo 7's own "throttle to Slow 3G" exercise) this would show the overlay disappearing while the Evidence catalogue is still stuck on its own separate "Loading evidence…" placeholder underneath it. Fix: bump the budget to 3 and add a `.finally(hideLoadingStep)` to loadEvidenceData's fetch chain, mirroring how loadTimelineData already does it — a minimal, self-contained fix that doesn't touch the surrounding `.then()`-chain structure. Note: this is deliberately narrower than a related, pre-existing issue — `loadAllData()`'s own returned Promise still resolves right after `loadCorePeopleAndLocations()`, not after all three steps, because `loadEvidenceData()`/`loadTimelineData()` are called without `return`/`await`. That's genuinely Demo 9 (.then() → async/await) scope and is deliberately left alone here; today's fix only corrects the *step counter*, not that ordering.

steps.title: D5 - T2 (1/2) — Live: the broken Sort dropdown (at pre-fix commit a8a97d7)
steps.narration: Chosen bug for the live demo: the Evidence catalogue sort (T1 4/7) — picked because it needs no localStorage setup, is 100% deterministic (not timing-sensitive like the loading-overlay bug), and has a single, easy-to-narrate root cause. To run this slide for real, check out the pre-fix commit first: `git checkout a8a97d7 -- js/views/evidence.js` (or check out the whole commit). On the Evidence view, with every filter left at its default, change "Sort evidence" to "Title (A–Z)". Expected: the 18 cards reorder alphabetically by title. Actual, at this commit: nothing happens — the list stays in original E01, E02, E03… order. handleSortChange() sorted state.filteredEvidence, then immediately called renderEvidenceList(), which rebuilt and reassigned state.filteredEvidence from scratch in unsorted order before a single frame rendered the sorted version.

steps.title: D5 - T2 (2/2) — Live: the fixed Sort dropdown (current code, commit 010050c)
steps.narration: Restore the fixed code (`git checkout main -- js/views/evidence.js`, or just be on main/010050c) and repeat the identical action: Evidence view, default filters, "Sort evidence" → "Title (A–Z)". Now the 18 cards visibly reorder alphabetically, starting with "Approved release manifest". To make the fix's robustness obvious, follow up by changing a filter (e.g. "Filter by status" → Unreviewed) without touching the sort dropdown again — the remaining cards stay in that same alphabetical order instead of reverting to unsorted, which is exactly the behavior that was silently broken before: applyCurrentSortOrder is now re-applied as the last step of every filter rebuild, not just the one render immediately after the dropdown changes.

steps.title: D5 - Q1 — Exact user actions and system state that trigger the chosen bug
steps.narration: Starting from pre-fix commit a8a97d7, with the app freshly loaded (state.allEvidence populated with all 18 items, state.evidenceViewLoading already false, every filter control at its untouched default — "All types", "All people", "All locations", "All statuses", "All relevance"): the ONLY action is changing the "Sort evidence" `<select>`'s value, e.g. to "title-asc". That fires its onchange handler, `handleSortChange()`, in js/views/evidence.js. Inside it: `state.filteredEvidence.sort(...)` runs first and genuinely does reorder the array in memory — for one brief moment the sort is real. But the very next line is `renderEvidenceList();`, and renderEvidenceList's first real step is `var results = getFilteredEvidence();`. getFilteredEvidence has no awareness that a sort was just requested — it loops over `state.allEvidence` (never touched, still in original E01–E18 order) applying only the filter controls, builds a fresh `results` array in that original order, and does `state.filteredEvidence = results;`, overwriting the just-sorted array with an unsorted one. renderEvidenceList then renders that overwritten `results`, so the sorted state that existed for a few microtask ticks is never once painted to the screen. This is deterministic, not a race: it happens on the very first interaction with the dropdown, every time, with no dependency on data size, network timing, or prior state.

steps.title: D5 - Q2 — Did fixing one bug affect another, and how was isolation confirmed
steps.narration: Honest answer, grounded in what I actually observed while testing: no cross-bug interactions among this demo's 7 new bugs. Each lives in an independent code path — a console.log call, a timeline string-formatting line, two separate JSON.parse call sites, the evidence filter/sort rebuild, a timeline modal's event listener, and a workspace dropdown rebuild — and none of the fixes touch code any other fix depends on. I confirmed this concretely, not just by assumption: after applying all 7 fixes together (not one at a time), I re-ran every single bug's own repro script again and checked each still passed exactly as it had in isolation — e.g. re-verifying the timeline location fix and the modal-leak fix didn't change each other's output, and that fixing the sort bug left the [object Object] fix's output untouched. The one real relationship I did find was WITHIN a single finding, not across two separate ones: the notes-storage crash and the hypothesis-storage crash are two independent instances of the identical bug pattern — an unguarded JSON.parse on hand-editable localStorage — not one causing the other. I explicitly didn't double-count them as two unrelated bugs; I noted the shared root-cause class and applied the same try/catch fix to both distinct locations. Separately, I confirmed the loadingStepsRemaining budget bug is NOT the same issue as the pre-existing "loadAllData doesn't await loadEvidenceData" ordering gap noted from a prior session (left for Demo 9): the budget fix is a simple off-by-one in a step counter; re-reading dataLoading.js after applying it confirms loadAllData()'s returned Promise still resolves right after loadCorePeopleAndLocations(), completely unchanged — the two issues are adjacent in the same function but genuinely independent.

steps.title: D6 - T1 — Real breakpoints in the Demo 3 bug's functions
steps.narration: Real debugging tool, not console.log: set two genuine breakpoints via the CDP Debugger domain (Debugger.setBreakpointByUrl), both inside functions from the Demo 3 async bug, against the pre-fix commit d1ed458 (Demo 3's fix, 7503cb0, doesn't exist yet at this commit). Breakpoint A: js/dataLoading.js:65, `state.allEvidence = data;` — inside loadEvidenceData()'s fetch-success callback. Breakpoint B: js/views/evidence.js:92, `if (state.evidenceViewLoading) {` — inside renderEvidenceList(). Reloading the app hit breakpoint A for real (confirmed via the paused event's own hitBreakpoints list), then I stepped through it line by line — see the next slide for the exact trace.

steps.title: D6 - T2 — Step Over / Into / Out, and the depth change that shows the difference
steps.narration: From the pause at dataLoading.js:65: Step Over moved to line 66 (`applyStoredBookmarkFlags();`) without descending — call-frame depth stayed the same. Step Into then entered applyStoredBookmarkFlags() itself, landing at js/views/evidence.js:173 — depth went 1→2, a new frame pushed. Step Out returned from that frame back to the caller, landing on js/dataLoading.js:75 (`state.filteredEvidence = state.allEvidence.slice();`, the next executable line after the call — the comment block in between is skipped) — depth back to 1. The 1→2→1 depth trace is the concrete, observable difference between the three.

steps.title: D6 - T3 — Call Stack: who called this, and with what
steps.narration: Two real examples. (a) At the dataLoading.js:65 pause, the async call stack (Debugger.setAsyncCallStackDepth) showed loadEvidenceData was itself called from the anonymous .then callback at js/dataLoading.js:109 — i.e. loadAllData()'s loadCorePeopleAndLocations().then(function () { loadEvidenceData(); loadTimelineData(); }). (b) At the evidence.js:92 pause, the synchronous call stack showed renderEvidenceList ← handleHashChange (js/navigation.js:60) — proving navigation here is driven by a hashchange listener, not directly by the nav button's onclick, since that click handler had already returned by the time this frame ran. Reading the stack, not just the source, is what surfaced that.

steps.title: D6 - T4 — Conditional breakpoint: only pause for item.id === 'E05'
steps.narration: Set a conditional breakpoint on js/views/evidence.js:73 (`if (matches) results.push(item);`, inside getFilteredEvidence()'s filter loop) with condition item.id === 'E05'. On resume, execution ran silently through the 4 preceding non-matching items (E01–E04) and paused exactly once, confirmed via Debugger.evaluateOnCallFrame reading { i: 4, id: "E05", title: "Nova Byte's chat message" } — the loop state was already correct in scope at the one iteration that mattered, no manual counting through Resume needed.

steps.title: D6 - T5 — Live-edit the paused scope to confirm the hypothesis before the fix
steps.narration: Paused at js/views/evidence.js:92, before the `if (state.evidenceViewLoading)` check runs, and read the paused scope: evaluateOnCallFrame('state.evidenceViewLoading') → true (the Demo 3 root cause, live: the fetch resolved but this flag was never reset). Live-edited it with evaluateOnCallFrame('state.evidenceViewLoading = false'), then resumed. Captured result: 18 .evidence-card elements actually rendered, loading indicator hidden, first card "Morning calibration failure report" — the hypothesis confirmed correctly before a single line of the real fix (already committed, at 7503cb0) was touched.

steps.title: D6 - Q1 — Step Over vs. Step Into, and where using the wrong one wastes time
steps.narration: Step Over executes the current line — including any function call on it — to completion without pausing inside it, staying at the same call-frame depth. Step Into descends into the first line of whatever function is called on the current line, pushing a new frame. Concrete example from this app: while debugging the Demo 3 bug inside loadEvidenceData()'s .then callback, stepping Into applyStoredBookmarkFlags() walks you through its bookmark-restoration loop over state.bookmarks/state.allEvidence — code with nothing to do with why evidenceViewLoading never gets reset. That wastes time; Step Over is correct there. Step Into is only worth it on that line if you suspect the bookmark restoration itself is broken, which for this bug it isn't.

steps.title: D6 - Q2 — What the call stack is, and what it revealed here
steps.narration: The call stack is the ordered chain of function invocations currently in progress at the paused moment — top frame is the function actually executing (paused), each frame below is the caller waiting for it to return, down to the outermost caller or, across an async gap, the recorded async origin. Reading it at the evidence.js:92 pause told me renderEvidenceList() had actually been called by handleHashChange, not by the nav button's click handler as reading the source top-to-bottom suggested — the real, indirect trigger was a hashchange listener reacting to navigateTo() setting location.hash.

steps.title: D6 - Q3 — Conditional breakpoints vs. repeatedly hitting Resume
steps.narration: A conditional breakpoint only actually pauses execution when a JS expression you supply evaluates truthy at that line — the engine still evaluates it on every hit but only stops the one time it's true. More efficient than resume-spamming: reaching item E05 in the 18-item getFilteredEvidence() loop by hand means hitting Resume 4 times and manually checking item.id at each stop — easy to miscount on a bigger catalogue. The conditional breakpoint let execution run past every non-matching item silently and land exactly once, with the loop state already correct and ready to inspect.

steps.title: D6 - Q4 — DevTools UI breakpoint vs. a `debugger;` statement
steps.narration: A UI/CDP breakpoint attaches to the running/served code without touching the source file — toggled per session, no deploy or edit needed, and (as this demo shows) fully scriptable via CDP. A debugger; statement is committed into the source itself — fires unconditionally whenever that line executes, in any environment with DevTools open (silent no-op otherwise), and needs an actual code change — plus remembering to remove it — to add or remove. Prefer UI/CDP for exploratory debugging like this demo, where I never touched the pre-fix source file, or whenever you shouldn't modify the file (this repo's pure-refactor discipline is a real example of that constraint). Prefer debugger; when the trigger is awkward to express as a DevTools condition, or the breakpoint needs to travel with the code with zero setup.

steps.title: D6 - Q5 — A moment console.log alone wouldn't have been enough
steps.narration: The live-edit step (T5) is exactly this moment. A console.log(state.evidenceViewLoading) inside renderEvidenceList() could only ever have told me the flag was true and stayed true — logging observes state, it can't change it. To actually confirm the hypothesis — if this flag were correctly reset to false, the catalogue would render — before writing the real fix, I needed to reach into the live paused scope and mutate state.evidenceViewLoading mid-execution, then watch the rest of the function run past the guard with the new value. Logging can tell you a value is wrong; only the debugger let me test what happens if it were right, live, before touching the actual code.

steps.title: D7 - DevTools tour: Console, Network, Application, Elements
steps.narration: A guided tour of where things live in DevTools, driven live against this running app via a real Chrome CDP session rather than screenshots of a separate panel — so every number and message on the next 8 slides is something that was actually captured, not described from memory. Console, Network, Application/Storage, and Elements each get one real, verified pass.

steps.title: D7 - T1 — Console: log-level filters, text filter, Preserve log
steps.narration: DevTools' log-level filter buttons key off exactly the field CDP's Runtime.consoleAPICalled reports as `type`. Filtering to Info: 6 real console.log entries from clicking every nav button ("nav clicked: evidence", js/main.js:44) plus "First note preview:" (main.js:86). Filtering to Warnings: corrupting localStorage key remotion_notes with invalid JSON and reloading produced a real console.warn — "Could not read stored notes, starting empty" with a full SyntaxError stack from js/storage.js:43. Filtering to Errors: forcing data/evidence.json to return a real 404 and reloading produced two real error-level entries, including the app's own console.error at js/dataLoading.js:89. The text filter box is just a substring match against the visible line list — filtering the captured events for "Could not read stored notes" isolates exactly that one warning. Preserve log has no page-JS-observable state, so it's described and confirmed against documented Chrome behavior rather than clicked: by default the Console panel clears on every navigation; Preserve Log keeps entries visible across reloads instead — and every capture here used a fresh listener per reload, which is exactly the default (Preserve Log OFF) behavior.

steps.title: D7 - T2 — Network: inspecting and throttling the JSON data requests
steps.narration: A real CDP Network session found all 5 data/*.json requests on a normal reload (case, people, locations, evidence, timeline — all 200/application/json), and pulled the full response body for data/evidence.json via Network.getResponseBody, starting with the real E01 record. Then throttled to Slow 3G (400kbps, 2000ms latency, Chrome's documented preset) via Network.emulateNetworkConditions and reloaded for real: case.json measured 2047ms, versus sub-1ms unthrottled — confirming Time here is dominated by the simulated latency floor, not payload size, since these files are tiny. What that throttled reload actually looked like on screen is Q4.

steps.title: D7 - T3 — Application: inspecting, editing, and corrupting localStorage
steps.narration: This app keeps 3 keys in localStorage (all defined in js/state.js): remotion_bookmarks, remotion_notes, remotion_hypothesis. After actually using the app — starring a card, saving a hypothesis draft — their real values were inspected live. Then, DevTools-panel-style, remotion_bookmarks was overwritten directly to ["E01","E05"] and the page reloaded: exactly those two cards rendered starred afterward, proving bookmarks are read from storage once at boot (loadBookmarksFromStorage), not kept live-synced. Separately, remotion_notes was overwritten with the literal invalid-JSON string "not valid json {{{" and reloaded — see Q3 for exactly what happened and why.

steps.title: D7 - T4 — Elements: tracing a rendered evidence card back to its code
steps.narration: The real rendered DOM for evidence card E01 was pulled via outerHTML and matched line-for-line against renderEvidenceCardHTML(ev) in js/views/evidence.js:148-168: the data-id and starred bookmark button come from checking ev.id against state.bookmarks; title, meta line, and summary are direct template interpolation of ev.title/ev.id/ev.type/formatDate(ev.timestamp)/ev.summary; the three badges come from getStatusBadgeClass()/getRelevanceBadgeClass() in js/lookup.js. Tracing this surfaced a real code smell: getRelevanceBadgeClass's fallback (lookup.js:56) reuses the same badge-unreviewed CSS class as the status badge, so two semantically different badges render identically styled — left for Demo 8's code-smell hunt, not fixed here, since this demo is a tour, not a bug hunt.

steps.title: D7 - Q1 — console.log vs. warn vs. error, beyond the color
steps.narration: Beyond color: each carries a distinct CDP type (log/warning/error) — exactly what DevTools' filter buttons and error/warning badge counters key off, not the rendered color. error/warn also attach a full stack trace; log doesn't unless you pass one explicitly — confirmed live, since the captured evidence.json console.error carried a real SyntaxError stack while the nav-click console.log entries carried none. And automated tooling — CI assertions, error trackers, this session's own CDP capture — typically watches error/warning types specifically and ignores log, so the choice determines whether a real problem is visible to anything beyond a human scrolling the panel.

steps.title: D7 - Q2 — Status/Type/Time, and what a 404 would actually do
steps.narration: For data/evidence.json: Status is the HTTP code (200 normally, 404 in the forced-failure test); Type is the request/response kind (fetch, application/json body); Time is sub-1ms unthrottled versus a real 2047ms under Slow 3G — latency-dominated since the payload is tiny. What a 404 does was confirmed live, not guessed: loadEvidenceData() in js/dataLoading.js never checks res.ok before calling .json(). A 404 with a non-JSON body throws a SyntaxError inside .json(), which the existing .catch() handles — logs console.error, shows an alert, and correctly resets state.evidenceViewLoading = false so the Evidence view falls back to its normal empty state instead of hanging on the loading placeholder forever. The Demo 3 fix holds even on this failure path.

steps.title: D7 - Q3 — localStorage keys, and why corrupting one doesn't crash the app
steps.narration: Three keys: remotion_bookmarks (bookmarked evidence IDs), remotion_notes (evidence ID to note text), remotion_hypothesis (the Workspace hypothesis draft) — all in js/state.js. Corrupting remotion_notes with invalid JSON and reloading, live: the app did not crash, specifically because loadNotesFromStorage() in js/storage.js wraps JSON.parse in a try/catch added during Demo 5's bug-fix pass, catches the SyntaxError, logs a real console.warn, and falls back to state.notesStore = {} in memory. Before that fix, this exact corruption threw uncaught during initApp() and aborted the entire boot sequence — the same failure class Demo 4 documented for a different function. The corrupted raw string itself is never auto-repaired in storage; only the in-memory fallback differs, confirmed by reading localStorage back after the reload. loadBookmarksFromStorage and loadHypothesisFromStorage carry the identical guard for the same reason.

steps.title: D7 - Q4 — What throttling revealed about load order
steps.narration: Under real Slow 3G throttle, nothing populated incrementally: the loading overlay's text stayed frozen on "Loading case file..." — set once at boot, never updated per-step — for 10+ measured seconds, with every part of the UI appearing at once only once all three loading steps (the sequential case.json to people.json to locations.json chain, then evidence and timeline) finished and hideLoadingStep()'s shared counter in js/dataLoading.js hit zero. Order matters because that core chain is sequential, not parallel — exactly what Demo 9 will refactor — so each step's throttled latency stacks on top of the last before the user sees anything at all: roughly 3x2000ms of the core chain alone under Slow 3G, before an all-or-nothing reveal. A real, observed UX cost of the current sequential architecture, noted here and left for Demo 9 rather than fixed now.

steps.title: D8 - T1 — The 18 original top-level `var`s, and 3 collision risks
steps.narration: This is the original pre-Demo-1 app.js: 18 bare top-level vars, all sharing one global function scope. Three explained: allEvidence — any function anywhere in the ~1085-line file could reassign it, or a second helper could silently reuse the name for something unrelated and clobber the canonical evidence list with no error. currentPage — generic enough that an independently-written view module could plausibly declare its own local currentPage believing it was private, silently shadowing the router's actual page tracker (contrast with currentPeopleTab, which the code deliberately keeps as its own separate concept rather than reusing currentPage). latestSearchRequestId — in the flat script there was no way to express "this counter is private to the search-input handler"; it lived at the same top-level scope as everything else. Demo 1's module split fixes all three differently: allEvidence and currentPage are now properties on one exported `state` object (js/state.js) — a property access can't collide with an unrelated bare name the way two same-named globals could; latestSearchRequestId became a genuinely module-private `let` inside js/views/evidence.js — true file-level privacy the flat script never had at all.

steps.title: D8 - T2 (1/2) — Sweeping all 171 `var`s to deliberate `const`/`let`
steps.narration: Swept all 10 js/*.js and js/views/*.js files — 171 var declarations total, zero left afterward (js/state.js already had zero, written as const/object-properties from the Demo 1 split itself). Rule applied per declaration, not blanket: let only where the binding is genuinely reassigned after its first assignment — every for-loop counter, accumulator strings built with +=, counters incremented with ++, and a couple of declare-now-assign-later bindings; const everywhere else, which was the large majority, since most of these var declarations held a single DOM lookup, a single computed value, or an array only ever pushed into (mutating an array's contents isn't reassigning the binding, so those stayed const). navigation.js's handleHashChange is a clean example: hash gets reassigned to "dashboard" a few lines down, so it needs let; validViews is built once and never reassigned, so it's const even though it's still just as mutable-looking as hash was as a var.

steps.title: D8 - T2 (2/2) — The one flagged behavior-affecting/syntax finding
steps.narration: Out of all 171, exactly one couldn't just default to const: js/views/workspace.js's loadHypothesisFromStorage originally had `var draft;` with no initializer, assigned only later inside a try block. `const draft;` with no initializer is a SyntaxError — const requires immediate initialization — confirmed directly with `node --check`, which failed until this was declared `let draft;` instead. Every other reassigned binding across the sweep got let as a deliberate choice, not because const was syntactically impossible — this is the only one where it actually was. Separately, Demo 4's existing let i fix for the nav-button loop closure bug (js/main.js) was left completely untouched by this sweep, and re-verified live afterward: clicking each nav button still logs its own correct data-view, not the last button's.

steps.title: D8 - T3 (1/2) — Code smell: relevance badges silently reusing status-badge styling
steps.narration: This was the Demo 7 lead, verified real rather than assumed: getRelevanceBadgeClass fell back to "badge-unreviewed" — a class that visually and semantically belongs to review-status badges. Every evidence item in data/evidence.json currently has relevance "Unknown", so this fallback fired on every single card — confirmed live via Playwright screenshot that the "UNREVIEWED" status pill and the "unknown" relevance pill rendered as the exact same solid grey badge, side by side, on every card. Two unrelated axes — has this been reviewed? vs. is this relevant? — made visually indistinguishable. Fix: a dedicated .badge-relevance-unclear CSS class, same neutral grey but with a dashed border instead of solid, so it reads as "unclear/pending" rather than borrowing status semantics. Verified live: the relevance badge now renders with a visibly dashed border distinct from the solid status pill, and switching an item's relevance to "Relevant" in the detail view still correctly switches it to badge-relevant.

steps.title: D8 - T3 (2/2) — Code smell: duplicate event-listener registrations
steps.narration: Two instances of the same root problem, both in main.js. First: #filterStatus was wired twice — once via addEventListener like every other filter control, and again via an inline setAttribute("onchange", "renderEvidenceList()") string, which existed only so that string could resolve renderEvidenceList off window — meaning every status-filter change re-ran the full catalogue render twice, and the function had to stay exported globally purely to support this one redundant path. Second: handleHashChange was registered as the hashchange listener twice — once inside setupEventListeners, once more at the bottom of the file — a duplication the code's own comments explicitly flagged as "reproduced from the original" and deliberately preserved through Demo 1's pure refactor. Neither produced a visible bug, which is exactly the cost: every navigation silently re-ran the entire view-render/nav-highlight logic twice, and for Workspace specifically (which always re-renders per its own comment) rebuilt the bookmarks list, notes list, and hypothesis dropdowns twice per hash change. Fix: removed both redundant registrations and the now-unnecessary window.renderEvidenceList export. Verified live: filterStatus's onchange attribute is now null, the filter still correctly filters (including combined with an active sort), and every nav path still renders exactly once.

steps.title: D8 - Q1 — var vs. let vs. const: scope, reassignment, and the Demo 4 example
steps.narration: Scope: var is function-scoped (or global at top level) and hoisted to undefined before its declaration line runs, ignoring block boundaries entirely; let/const are block-scoped, confined to the nearest {...}, and sit in a temporal dead zone that throws a ReferenceError if read before their declaration actually executes. Reassignment: var and let can both be reassigned any number of times; const can be assigned only once, at declaration — confirmed live: const x = 1; x = 2; throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable at runtime, not caught by node --check, which is exactly why every reassignment in the T2 sweep was hand-verified rather than trusted to a syntax check alone. Concrete bug var makes possible and let prevents: this app's own Demo 4 fix, still visible right here in main.js's nav-button loop — with var i, every button's click closure would read the loop's shared, final value after the loop finished, so every button reported the last button's data-view; let gives each iteration its own binding, so each closure captures its own button correctly. Re-verified live this session: clicking each nav button still logs its own correct data-view.

steps.title: D8 - Q2 — Accidental globals, and what ES modules' strict mode does instead
steps.narration: An accidental global is what happens in non-strict (sloppy-mode) JavaScript when code assigns to a bare, undeclared name inside a function — instead of erroring, the engine silently creates a new property on the global object (window in a browser) and assigns there. That global was never declared on purpose, is invisible to anyone reading just that function's signature, and can silently collide with any other same-named variable anywhere else in the program — exactly the class of risk the original app.js globals carried. ES modules are always strict mode, with no opt-out, so the same mistake behaves completely differently — verified live, not just asserted: loaded a throwaway module (`export function oops() { accidentallyGlobal = 42; }`) via a Blob URL and called it in the running app's page context. Result: ReferenceError: accidentallyGlobal is not defined, thrown immediately at the assignment, with no property ever created on window. The module system doesn't just make the existing globals in this app safer — it turns the exact keyword-forgetting mistake that created those globals in the first place into an immediate, loud crash instead of a silent one.

steps.title: D8 - Q3 — "It works" vs. "it's clean": the #filterStatus double-registration
steps.narration: The #filterStatus double-registration from T3 is exactly this case: it worked — every status-filter change did correctly re-filter the evidence list, with no visible bug, for seven demos straight before anyone flagged it. But the messy version had real, non-hypothetical cost. Bug risk: renderEvidenceList had to stay exported to window solely to support the redundant inline-string path — exactly the kind of leftover surface that makes a future rename or removal silently break something invisible and far away. Onboarding/review difficulty: a reviewer reading setupEventListeners sees filterStatus wired once via addEventListener and has no reason to suspect a second, functionally-identical wiring exists two lines later via a string attribute — it was only caught now, in a dedicated code-smell pass, not during any of the seven prior demos' adversarial walkthroughs, because "the filter still works" gave no visible signal anything was wrong. Compounding cost: the identical pattern — handleHashChange registered twice — had already independently crept into the same file. That's what "technically works, not clean" actually costs over time: the same category of smell recurs because nothing about "it works" ever forces anyone to notice or remove it.

steps.title: D9 - T1 — Sketching the 6-level nested `.then()` chain
steps.narration: Before touching anything: loadCorePeopleAndLocations() was the deepest nested chain in the app — 6 levels, one fetch+json.then pair each for case.json, people.json, locations.json, each nested strictly inside the previous one's callback. None of these three resources actually depend on each other's data — they're independent files — but the chain's shape forced them to load one after another anyway, because that's the only order a nested .then() chain naturally expresses: people.json's fetch() call is textually and temporally inside case.json's .then(), so it can't start until that callback runs, and locations.json is nested one level deeper still. The final render/overlay-hiding code sits at the innermost level, six callbacks deep, gated on all three having resolved in exactly that order.

steps.title: D9 - T2 — Converting `loadCorePeopleAndLocations` to `async`/`await`
steps.narration: Each await below is exactly one rung of the old nested chain, in the same order — case fetched and parsed, then people fetched and parsed, then locations fetched and parsed, then the render/overlay step. The sequential behavior is preserved exactly on purpose: people's fetch still doesn't start until both of case's awaits have resolved, and locations still waits on people — parallelizing this is explicitly out of scope until a later exercise. No try/catch was added either, because the original chain had none — a rejection still just propagates out as a rejected Promise, unchanged. What actually changes is readability: one indent level instead of six, and no more separate callback scopes to track a value's handoff through.

steps.title: D9 - T3 — Second conversion: `loadEvidenceData`, with `try`/`catch`/`finally`
steps.narration: The second required .then()-chain conversion: loadEvidenceData(), which had the app's richest error handling (.catch + .finally). Converted to async/await with try/catch/finally doing exactly what the original did — same console.error, same alert, same evidenceViewLoading reset on failure, same hideLoadingStep() in finally regardless of outcome. One side effect worth calling out: this function previously had no `return` at all in front of its fetch chain, so calling it returned undefined, not a Promise. As an async function it now always returns a real Promise — which is what let loadAllData() below properly await it for the first time, fixing a dangling-promise gap flagged back in Demo 3/5 as a natural consequence of doing the conversion properly, not a separate bug fix.
