steps.title: D9 - Q1 — Why the nested chain is harder to reason about
steps.narration: Two concrete reasons, both visible in the T1/T2 diff. First, indentation tracks nothing meaningful in the nested version — six levels deep by the time you reach the actual render call, purely because that's how many .then()s came before it, not because the logic itself is six layers of complexity. The async/await version stays at one indent level for the whole sequential story. Second, each .then() callback is a brand-new anonymous function with its own closure scope, so following one value (like caseJson) across the chain means tracking which nested scope you're in and whether each level correctly `return`s its inner promise to the next .then(). Miss a return and the chain silently breaks — which is exactly the historical loadEvidenceData bug in this same file (Demo 3/5): a missing return meant its caller had no way to know when — or whether — the fetch had actually finished. await reads like ordinary synchronous assignment, so there's no return-to-pass-it-on convention to forget. Both versions run identically — this is a pure readability difference, not a behavioral one (see Q5).

steps.title: D9 - Q2 — What `await` actually does to execution
steps.narration: await pauses execution of only the async function it's inside, at that exact line, until the awaited Promise settles — but it does NOT block the JS engine's single thread. Execution unwinds back out of the async function to whatever called it, exactly as if the function had reached the end of its synchronous portion; the rest of the program — other event handlers, timers, rendering, unrelated Promises — keeps running normally the whole time. Once the awaited Promise settles, the function's remaining body is scheduled to resume as a microtask. The debugger trace from T4 shows the very start of this directly: at the first await (before it had even settled), the sync call stack still showed loadCorePeopleAndLocations <- loadAllData <- initApp with nothing extra queued — because at that exact instant nothing had suspended yet; the suspend/resume only becomes observable once that first await's Promise actually settles and hands control back to just this function's continuation.

steps.title: D9 - Q3 — An `async` function always returns a Promise
steps.narration: Proven live in the running app (Playwright browser_evaluate against the real page): imported js/dataLoading.js and called the real refactored loadAllData(). `loadAllData() instanceof Promise` -> true. Calling `.then(v => v)` on it and logging the resolved value gave `undefined` — because loadAllData()'s body has no explicit return statement, so its implicit return value is undefined, but it's still genuinely wrapped in a real Promise object, not handed back directly. To prove the other half unambiguously — that even an explicit `return someValue` for a plain value still gets Promise-wrapped — also ran an isolated snippet in the same page: `async function demoReturnsPlainValue() { return 42; }` -> instanceof Promise -> true, and `.then(v => v)` resolved to 42, not a synchronously-returned 42. You always have to unwrap it.

steps.title: D9 - Q4 — The `async`/`await` equivalent of `.catch()`
steps.narration: try { await somePromise; } catch (err) { ... } — exactly what got applied to loadEvidenceData() in T3. Verified live what happens if you forget it: defined an async function that awaits a Promise.reject(...), and called it WITHOUT await or a try/catch around the call — the genuine "forgot the catch" scenario. Captured a real window unhandledrejection event firing with the actual error's message, and the browser's own console logged a real "Uncaught (in promise) Error" with a full stack trace. So the rejection doesn't vanish and doesn't crash the script either — it surfaces as an unhandled Promise rejection, the same class of signal a thrown error in a .then() chain with no .catch() would produce, just reported through the unhandledrejection event / console instead of stopping execution at the await site (the awaiting function has already suspended and control has moved on by the time it fires).

steps.title: D9 - Q5 — Is `async`/`await` faster than `.then()`? No.
steps.narration: No — and the T4 debugger trace is direct proof: the actual sequence of operations (fetch case, parse case, assign, fetch people, parse people, assign, fetch locations, parse locations, assign, render) is identical, in the identical order, to what the nested .then() chain did. async/await is syntax sugar over the same Promise machinery — the engine still suspends the function at each await and resumes it as a microtask once the underlying Promise settles, the exact mechanism .then() uses underneath. Nothing changes about the number of requests, their relative timing, or total wall-clock time — this refactor is purely about how the same execution is written and read, not how it executes. Actually making it faster would mean changing WHAT gets awaited and WHEN — e.g. Promise.all to run independent fetches concurrently — which stays deliberately out of scope here per the Task 2 instruction to preserve sequential behavior exactly.

steps.title: D9 - Q6 — Deliberately breaking the refactor by dropping an `await`
steps.narration: Temporarily changed `const caseJson = await caseRes.json();` to `const caseJson = caseRes.json();` — dropped the await, function still async — reloaded the real app, and confirmed live: state.caseData held an actual Promise object (Object.prototype.toString -> "[object Promise]"), not the parsed case data. Real, visible breakage followed: the Dashboard's case header fell back to its default placeholder "Case" instead of "Project ReMotion – Investigation Portal", and the status badge showed "UNKNOWN" instead of "OPEN" — because dashboard.js reads caseData.title/.status off what's actually a pending Promise, and that property access just silently returns undefined, which the render code falls back on. Restored the await immediately after and reconfirmed the fix (title and OPEN both back). This is precisely the same bug category as the Demo 3/5 loadEvidenceData issue in this very file: a Promise read as if it were already the resolved value — there a missing `return` silently discarded a Promise's completion signal, here a missing `await` left a Promise object sitting where real data was expected. Same root mistake, opposite syntax.

steps.title: D10 - T1 (1/2) — `certaintyBadgeClass` to an arrow function
steps.narration: First arrow-function conversion: certaintyBadgeClass in timeline.js. It's a pure module-private lookup — no this, no arguments, never used as a constructor — called only from renderTimeline in the same file, so it's a clean candidate. Converted from a function declaration to a const arrow function. Behaviorally identical: verified live after the change by reloading the Timeline view and confirming all 15 rendered events still carry the correct badge class per certainty (confirmed to reviewed, contradictory to critical, reported to flagged, everything else to unreviewed).

steps.title: D10 - T1 (2/2) — `statCardHTML` to an arrow function
steps.narration: Second good candidate: statCardHTML in dashboard.js, a pure template-string helper called five times from renderDashboard to build the stat-card row. Same reasoning as certaintyBadgeClass — no this/arguments/constructor use, module-private, only called at runtime after the module has fully evaluated. Verified live: reloaded the Dashboard and confirmed all five stat cards (18 Evidence items, 6 People, 6 Locations, 0 Bookmarked, 1 Reviewed) still render with the same markup and values as before the conversion.

steps.title: D10 - T2 — anonymous `addEventListener` callback to an arrow function
steps.narration: The required addEventListener conversion: the hypConfidence range slider's input listener in main.js, previously an anonymous function(e) {...}. It only reads e.target.value and writes it into the confidence-value output — no this, nothing that needs a fresh binding per call. Converted to an arrow function. Verified live: set the slider's value to 77 and dispatched a real input event — hypConfidenceValue's text updated to "77", identical to the pre-conversion behavior.

steps.title: D10 - T3 — deliberately NOT converted: `handleEvidenceListClick`
steps.narration: The one function I deliberately left as a function declaration: handleEvidenceListClick in evidence.js. It's registered directly by reference — container.addEventListener("click", handleEvidenceListClick), not wrapped in another callback — implementing click-delegation over the evidence card list. A function attached this way is called by the DOM with this bound to the listening element (container), which is the actual contract of the delegated-click pattern here. This version reads event.target rather than this, but converting it to an arrow function would permanently and silently discard that binding, since an arrow function always captures this from its enclosing module scope (undefined, strict mode) instead of whatever the caller supplies — foreclosing a very standard DOM pattern for anyone maintaining this function later. Verified the unconverted function still works correctly: clicking a card's bookmark button toggles state.bookmarks via delegation without triggering the card's own detail-open handler, and clicking the card body itself still opens that evidence's detail view.

steps.title: D10 - Q1 — Arrow `this` vs. regular-function `this`
steps.narration: A regular function gets its own this, determined dynamically by how it's called: obj.method() binds it to obj, addEventListener binds it to the listening element, a bare call leaves it undefined in strict mode. An arrow function has no this of its own — it lexically inherits this from whatever scope surrounds it at definition time, and that binding can never be overridden, not even by call/apply/bind. That's exactly why handleEvidenceListClick (T3) has to stay a declaration: it's registered as a DOM handler specifically so the browser can bind this to the listening element, the 'object method' pattern arrow functions break by design. It's preferable for callbacks, like the hypConfidence listener converted in T2, precisely because most callbacks don't want caller-determined this at all — they want to keep meaning whatever this meant in the surrounding code, which arrows give you by default instead of requiring a manual .bind(this).

steps.title: D10 - Q2 — Did the `new`/`arguments` limitations affect any conversion?
steps.narration: No — confirmed by grepping the whole js/ tree for `new <CustomName>(` and for `arguments`: zero hits beyond the built-in new Date()/new Promise()/new Error() calls already in the codebase, and zero uses of the arguments object anywhere — every function here takes named parameters. So neither limitation disqualified any candidate; the real disqualifying factor for handleEvidenceListClick was this-binding (Q1/T3), not arguments or new. The honest answer is that this codebase simply doesn't use either feature.

steps.title: D10 - Q3 — Did hoisting matter anywhere in this refactor?
steps.narration: It mattered enough to check carefully, but didn't block either T1 conversion. Both certaintyBadgeClass and statCardHTML are declared after, textually, the function that calls them (renderTimeline/renderDashboard) — but hoisting only matters for when a reference is actually evaluated, not where a function is textually defined relative to its caller's declaration. renderTimeline's body doesn't run when renderTimeline is declared, only when something later calls renderTimeline() — by which point the whole module's top-level code, including the const line below it, has already finished executing. So the real question is 'is this function ever called before its own const line has run?' — and for both, it isn't. This would matter if a function were called from another function's own top-level module-scope statements before its declaration line ran; neither candidate hit that case.

steps.title: D10 - Q4 — Before/after: behavioral difference or pure style?
steps.narration: Using certaintyBadgeClass as the concrete example (same before/after shown in T1): purely a readability/binding-form change, no runtime difference — verified live by reloading the Timeline view and confirming all 15 rendered badges map exactly as before the conversion. It's purely style here specifically because none of the three things that would make it behavioral apply to this function: it's never called before its own line runs (Q3), it never used this/arguments/new (Q2), and it's module-private either way, so there's no export-binding difference. Same inputs, same outputs, same call sites, same scope — only the syntax changed.

steps.title: D10 - Q5 — Proposed team rule for declarations vs. expressions vs. arrows
steps.narration: Proposed rule, as a single binary test per function: use a named function declaration only if the function is called by something else's this binding (registered directly by reference as a DOM/framework event handler, or ever attached as an object method) or genuinely needs to be callable before its own declaration line runs in the same scope — otherwise, use a const arrow function. In this codebase that keeps handleEvidenceListClick and the other directly-referenced addEventListener targets (renderEvidenceList, clearFilters, renderTimeline as change handlers) as declarations, since they're real or plausible-future DOM-this recipients; everything else — module-private helpers and one-off callbacks — becomes an arrow function. This gives two engineers the same answer without relying on taste, and it's mechanically checkable from a diff: does this function appear as a bare reference in an addEventListener call, or is it invoked before its own declaration executes?

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — What a package manager solves that manual download doesn't
steps.narration: Manually downloading a library means manually tracking its own dependencies (and their versions), re-doing that by hand every time a version changes, and having no single source of truth for what's actually installed. npm resolves the full dependency graph (Vite alone pulls in ~15 packages transitively), dedupes shared sub-dependencies, and records the exact resolved tree in package-lock.json — none of which "put it in a folder yourself" gives you.

steps.title: D1 - Q2 — dependencies vs devDependencies
steps.narration: dependencies ship inside the built app the user's browser actually runs; devDependencies are only needed while building/testing/linting on a developer's or CI machine. Vite, ESLint, Prettier and TypeScript are all devDependencies here — none of their code ends up in dist/, they only transform/check the source before it gets there. This app currently has zero runtime dependencies (no framework), so the dependencies field stays empty.

steps.title: D1 - Q3 — What a lockfile is for
steps.narration: A lockfile pins the exact resolved version (and sub-dependency versions) of everything installed, not just the semver ranges in package.json. Without it committed, a teammate (or CI) running npm install later could resolve a newer transitive version that behaves differently — works on my machine, breaks in CI is exactly the failure mode a missing lockfile invites.

steps.title: D1 - Q4 — What npm gives up vs pnpm on a larger project
steps.narration: pnpm keeps one global content-addressable store on disk and hard-links packages into each project's node_modules, so ten projects using the same Vite version store it once, not ten times, and installs are faster since most packages are already on disk. npm duplicates full copies per project. On a single small repo like this one the difference is negligible; on a machine running many Node projects (like this one, per Developer/CLAUDE.md's project list) it would add up — a legitimate reason to reconsider pnpm later, just not the deciding factor here.

steps.narration: To prove the gate really blocks, formatDate()'s declared return type was changed from string to number while its body still returns strings. Running npm run build stops at the typecheck step with three TS2322 errors (lines 62, 64 and 65 — every return statement) and vite build never runs. steps.title: D5 - Q1 — What strict actually turns on
steps.narration: strict bundles several independent checks — strictNullChecks (null/undefined must be handled explicitly, not silently assignable to everything) and noImplicitAny (every value needs an inferable or declared type, not a silent any) are the two that mattered most here. Kept both on: they're exactly what would have caught Exercise 1's undefined-access and implicit-any bugs at compile time instead of runtime.

steps.title: D5 - Q2 — Compile-time errors vs Exercise 1's runtime bugs
steps.narration: A compile-time type error is caught before the code ever runs, by static analysis of the declared shapes; Exercise 1's bugs (a stale var closure, a dropped await, a shared array reference) were all caught by actually running the code and observing wrong behavior. TypeScript alone would NOT have caught most of them — a stale closure and a shared array reference are both perfectly type-correct, wrong only in runtime timing/aliasing, which types don't model. It likely would have caught the dropped-await bug, since an un-awaited async call used where a value was expected produces a Promise<T> vs T mismatch.

steps.title: D5 - Q3 — What any does, and why avoid it even though it's faster
steps.narration: any opts a value out of type checking entirely — every property access, call, and assignment on it is accepted with zero verification, and that unchecked-ness silently spreads to anything the any value touches. Reaching for it would have been faster in the moment, but it would have made this exact TS setup unable to catch the bugs it exists to catch — an any-typed state.js export flowing into lookup.ts would make every one of its consumers unchecked too.

steps.title: D1 - T1 — Evolution of the web and where this app sits
steps.narration: Static documents, then server-rendered multi-page apps (PHP/JSP), then AJAX and jQuery, then SPA frameworks, then hybrid rendering. This app sits between AJAX and SPA frameworks: one HTML document, content created by client JS from fetched JSON — but no framework, so innerHTML string building, a global state object and a hand-written hashchange router. That is how SPAs were built before declarative UI libraries.

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — What AJAX solved and what it introduced
steps.narration: Solved: any interaction needing fresh data forced a full request and reload, losing scroll, focus and UI state. AJAX/jQuery fetched just the data and patched part of the DOM. New problems: you update every dependent DOM spot by hand (renderDashboard is called from four places here), state is scattered between DOM and globals, URL and history stop matching the screen, and there is no component model. SPA frameworks answered with declarative rendering, components and routers.

steps.title: D1 - Q2 — Hash routing: which era?
steps.narration: Early SPA era, roughly 2008–2013. Changing only the fragment is the one URL change that does not reload the page, so it was the only way to get reload-free navigation and a working back button before the History API (pushState) became reliable around 2012. It tells us client-side routing became common once browsers could change the URL without reloading. A hash is never sent to the server, so such routes cannot be server-rendered or indexed per view.

steps.title: D2 - T1 — SSR vs CSR comparison
steps.narration: SSR: first response is complete HTML with content, browser just parses and paints, later navigation is another document request. CSR: first response is an almost empty shell plus script tags; the browser must download and run JS, then fetch data, then build the DOM (HTML → JS → JSON waterfall); later navigation swaps views in place with at most a small JSON request. CSR is cheap to host and snappy afterwards; SSR wins on first paint, no-JS users and crawlers.

steps.title: D2 - T2 — Wikipedia is primarily SSR
steps.narration: Evidence from curl on en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Server-side_scripting, equivalent to view-source: a 133 KB HTML document whose paragraphs, headings and title are already in the raw response, only a handful of enhancing script tags, and no JSON call carrying the article in the network tab. Following a link triggers a new document request with a complete new HTML response — classic server-rendered navigation.

steps.title: D2 - Q1 — This app is CSR: path to a visible Dashboard
steps.narration: index.html contains an empty #dashboardContent with the comment rendered by app.js. Steps: server returns index.html unchanged → parser hits the stylesheet and module script → browser loads the module graph → initApp reads localStorage and calls loadAllData → fetches case, people, locations, then evidence and timeline in parallel → each step writes into state and calls renderDashboard, which sets innerHTML → overlay hides and handleHashChange shows the Dashboard. steps.title: D2 - Q2 — A real cost of CSR
steps.narration: Everything the user sees depends on JavaScript and several round trips. With JS disabled: header, dead nav, empty page, loading overlay forever, no noscript fallback. Slow connection: HTML + bundle + five JSON requests before content, where SSR could paint on the first response. Crawlers that skip JS index an empty shell, and hash routes are never even seen by the server. Acceptable here because nobody needs to find this tool through search.

steps.title: D3 - T1 — What the virtual DOM is
steps.narration: The real DOM is the browser live element tree; replacing subtrees is costly and throws away focus, scroll and typed text. The virtual DOM is a cheap in-memory description of the UI as plain objects. On each state change a new description is built, diffed against the previous one, and only the minimal real DOM operations are applied. It solves how to write render everything from state without paying for rebuilding the whole real DOM or hand-writing the which-nodes-changed logic.

It also re-adds the click listener on every render. steps.title: D3 - Q1 — How a virtual DOM avoids the rebuild
steps.narration: After the click the library produces a new virtual tree where 17 cards are identical and one has a different className and icon text. steps.title: D3 - Q2 — Is the virtual DOM faster than innerHTML?
steps.narration: Not inherently — it is a trade. Diffing is extra CPU and memory on top of the eventual DOM writes; a hand-written classList.toggle beats it, and a one-off full replacement via the native HTML parser can too. What you buy is a good worst case and a simple model: write render everything from state, get small DOM updates. You trade diffing cost for less DOM churn and far less hand-written update code.

steps.title: D3 - Q3 — Does a virtual DOM make an app fast?
steps.narration: No. React apps are still slow with excessive re-renders from state placed too high, expensive work in render instead of useMemo, missing or unstable keys that defeat the diff, huge lists without windowing, large bundles and request waterfalls (untouched by the virtual DOM), and effects that set state in loops.

steps.title: D4 - T2 — State lost on reload vs preserved
steps.narration: Preserved: bookmarks, notes and the saved hypothesis (localStorage), and the current view (URL hash). Lost: all fetched data (re-fetched on boot), evidence filters/search/sort, the open evidence detail, the People/Locations tab, timeline filters, unsaved hypothesis edits, viewRendered flags and loading flags — everything that lives only in memory or DOM control values.

steps.title: D4 - Q1 — Where does the current page data live?
steps.narration: MPA: on the server (database, session) and in the request (URL, cookies, form post); the client is stateless between requests. SPA: in browser memory (the state object here) and browser storage; the server only serves data. Good: instant navigation, no refetching, UI state survives view changes, simple cacheable server. Bad: state is lost on reload unless persisted, can go stale (the vanilla dashboard bug), is not shareable via URL, and two tabs diverge.

steps.title: D4 - Q2 — What a router library adds

steps.title: D5 - Q1 — What is JSX?
steps.narration:
JSX is syntax sugar for function calls, not HTML and not a string. With the automatic runtime,

Case {id}

becomes jsxs("p", { children: ["Case ", jsx("strong", { children: id })] }); the classic form is React.createElement. Each call returns a plain object, a React element — so a component returns a tree of objects that React diffs before touching the DOM. Vite plugin-react and tsconfig jsx react-jsx do this.

steps.title: D5 - Q2 — How each output becomes real DOM
steps.narration: String version: text goes into innerHTML and the browser HTML parser rebuilds all nodes every time, replacing what was there; the app keeps no representation of the result. Component version: React elements are objects in memory; React keeps the previous tree, diffs, and calls DOM APIs (createElement, className, textContent) only for differences. Values go in as text nodes and properties, so nothing is interpreted as markup.

steps.title: D5 - Q3 — Components are just functions
steps.narration: A component is (props) => UI and React expects it pure. React may call it more than once (StrictMode double-invokes in dev), pause or discard renders (concurrent rendering), or skip it. A render-time side effect — mutating a global, localStorage write, fetch — runs an unpredictable number of times, makes components order-dependent, shows inconsistent UI between components sharing the global, and leaves effects of renders the user never saw. Effects belong in event handlers and useEffect.

steps.title: D8 - T1 — ADR: is an SPA with React right for this app?
steps.narration: Recommended: keep the SPA, render it with React + TypeScript. The app is interaction-heavy (filter, sort, bookmark, notes, hypothesis), data is small static JSON, state is client-held in localStorage, there is no backend, and no SEO or first-paint pressure. React removes the stale-render and duplicated-markup bug classes seen in Exercises 1 and 3. Full text: docs/exercise-3/04-adr-spa-react.md.

steps.title: D8 - T2 — Honest downsides
steps.narration: React bundle is about 227 kB (71 kB gzip) versus about 20 kB for the whole vanilla app — roughly 11 times more JS for the same screen. More tooling and dependencies, CSR costs remain (blank without JS, waterfall, nothing for crawlers), hooks have their own bug classes, it is arguably overkill for 1.8k lines, and the migration leaves a split codebase until Exercise 5. Alternatives: server-rendered MPA, Preact or Svelte, Astro/Next if SEO or SSR ever matter.

steps.title: D8 - Q1 — What each alternative would lose
steps.narration: Server-rendered vanilla loses instant reload-free interaction (filters, open detail and notes UI reset), a single place for shared state, and component reuse — but gains tiny payloads, no-JS operation and crawlability. React over another SPA approach loses size and startup (about 70 kB gzip vs about 4 kB Preact or near zero compiled), simplicity (build step, JSX, hooks rules) and direct control over updates — but gains ecosystem, teaching standard and best TypeScript tooling.

steps.title: D8 - Q2 — Low-end devices as a hard requirement
steps.narration: I would change the architecture: a CSR SPA puts download, parse, execute, fetch and render cost on exactly the device and network least able to pay. First choice is prerendering or SSG the content with selective hydration of the interactive parts (islands, e.g. Astro); then a lighter client (Preact or plain TS, route-level code splitting); then fewer round trips by inlining critical JSON and caching with a service worker. The requirement flips the priority from interactivity to first meaningful paint on weak hardware.

steps.title: D1 - Q4 — Why direct DOM manipulation conflicts with React
steps.narration: React assumes it owns the DOM under its root: the component tree is the single description of what should be on screen, and on each render React diffs the new description against its last one and patches only the difference. If code outside React does innerHTML, appendChild or classList.add, React does not know. Its picture of the DOM is now wrong, so the next patch can target nodes that no longer exist, overwrite your change, or keep stale nodes, and event listeners attached to replaced nodes vanish. Vanilla renderPeople did the opposite: it rebuilt a string, replaced all children with innerHTML, and then re-attached listeners by hand. In React you describe the result for the current data and let React do the DOM work. This is why this exercise has the hard rules: no innerHTML, no createElement.

steps.title: D2 - T2 — Which conditional technique where, and why

Early return null: when a component has nothing to show, so it bails out at the top (ResponsibilityList) and the body stays unconditional. Lookup object: when the condition is a key into a fixed set, e.g. TAB_LABELS[tab]; a Record<PeopleTab, string> makes the compiler demand an entry for any new tab, which an if/else chain would not. I avoided nested ternaries, they are the thing that makes JSX unreadable.

steps.title: D3 - Q1 — What React uses key for
steps.narration: key tells React which element in the new list corresponds to which element in the previous render. During reconciliation, React compares the children of the same parent by key: same key means the same component instance, so it is kept (with its DOM node and any internal state) and just updated; a new key means mount, a missing key means unmount; a moved key means the node is moved instead of rebuilt. Without keys React falls back to position, which is only correct if the list never reorders. The key is not passed to the component as a prop (props.key is undefined), and it only needs to be unique among siblings, not globally.

# Exercise 4 — Presentational vs. feature components (Demo 5)

**Rule used:** a component is *presentational* if everything it renders arrives through its props
or `children` (same props in, same output), and it never reads context, fetches, touches
`localStorage` or `window.location`. It is a *feature* (container) component if it knows where
data comes from or how domain data is derived (context, URL, sorting, matching), and hands the
result down as props.

| Component | Kind | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `App` | feature (composition root) | Reads the current route, chooses the page, mounts the data provider |
| `CaseDataProvider` | feature (infrastructure) | Fetches the five JSON files, owns loading/error/ready |
| `Header`, `Footer`, `HowToUseCard`, `StubPage` | presentational | Static markup / props only |
| `NavBar` | presentational (with one callback-style dependency) | Gets `currentView` as a prop; the click calls `navigateTo`, a plain function — becomes a router link in Demo 8 |
| `DashboardPage`, `DashboardContent` | feature | Read context and localStorage, derive counts and recent lists |
| `CaseSummaryCard`, `StatGrid`, `StatCard`, `ReviewProgress`, `RecentEvidenceList`, `RecentTimelineList` | presentational | Props in, markup out |
| `PeoplePage`, `PeopleContent` | feature | Read context and the URL, match evidence to people |
| `PeopleLocationsView` | presentational | **Result of the split.** Tab, lists and counts all via props |
| `TabBar`, `Card`, `PersonCard`, `LocationCard`, `ResponsibilityList` | presentational | Props / children only |
| `TimelinePage`, `TimelineContent` | feature | Read context, sort events, resolve location labels, build filter options |
| `TimelineView` | presentational | **Result of the split.** Receives sorted entries and option lists |
| `TimelineItem`, `TimelineToolbar`, `FilterSelect` | presentational | Props only (toolbar controls are uncontrolled until Exercise 5) |
| `CaseBadge`, `KeyedPersonList` (sandbox) | presentational | Throwaway demos, not mounted in the app |

## The split

`PeoplePage` used to do four jobs in one tree: gate on loading/error, read the tab from the URL,
count evidence per person, and lay out tab bar plus cards. It is now:

- `PeopleContent` (feature): data and URL in, `activeTab` / `people` / `locations` /
  `evidenceCountByPersonId` out.
- `PeopleLocationsView` (presentational): layout and conditional rendering only.

`TimelinePage` got the same treatment (`TimelineContent` and `TimelineView`).

# Architecture

## React source layout (`react/`) — added in Exercise 4, Demo 6

The React app is organised **by feature**, not by file type.

```
react/
  main.tsx                      entry point mounted by react.html
  app/
    App.tsx                     composition root: provider + shell + route table
  shell/                        the frame around every page
    Header.tsx  NavBar.tsx  Footer.tsx  StubPage.tsx
  features/
    dashboard/                  everything only the Dashboard needs
      DashboardPage.tsx  StatGrid.tsx  CaseSummaryCard.tsx  ReviewProgress.tsx
      RecentEvidenceList.tsx  RecentTimelineList.tsx  HowToUseCard.tsx  bookmarks.ts
    people-locations/
      PeoplePage.tsx (feature)  PeopleLocationsView.tsx (presentational)
      PersonCard.tsx  LocationCard.tsx  Card.tsx  TabBar.tsx  ResponsibilityList.tsx
    timeline/
      TimelinePage.tsx (feature)  TimelineView.tsx (presentational)
      TimelineItem.tsx  TimelineToolbar.tsx
  shared/                       used by more than one feature
    data/CaseDataContext.tsx
    routing/useHashRoute.ts
  sandbox/                      throwaway teaching demos, not part of the app
```

Domain types and helpers (`js/types.ts`, `js/lookup.ts`) are still imported from the vanilla
`js/` folder, because the vanilla app keeps running next to the React one (`index.html` vs
`react.html`).

### Rule: shared vs. feature-local

1. A file lives **inside the one feature that uses it**, however generic it looks. Example:
   `Card.tsx` is a generic children-based box, but only `people-locations` uses it, so it stays
   in `features/people-locations/`.
2. It moves to **`shared/`** when a **second feature** needs it (or when it is app-wide
   infrastructure). Examples: `CaseDataContext.tsx` is read by Dashboard, People & Locations and
   Timeline, so it lives in `shared/data/`; `useHashRoute.ts` is used by the shell (NavBar,
   App) and by the Dashboard's HowToUseCard, so it lives in `shared/routing/`.
3. Dependencies point one way: `app` -> `features` -> `shared`. A feature never imports from
   another feature; if two features need the same thing, that is the signal to promote it to
   `shared/`.
4. `shell/` is not a feature: it is the frame (header, navigation, footer) that
   hosts the features.

Why by feature for this app: the three migrated views barely share UI (a person card is of no
use on the timeline) but each view's files change together, so a change to the Timeline touches
one folder. A by-type layout (`components/`, `hooks/`, `pages/`) would put 20 unrelated components
in one folder.

See also: `docs/exercise-3/03-component-hierarchy.md` (planned tree) and
`docs/exercise-4/05-component-classification.md` (presentational vs. feature).

steps.title: D6 - Q1 — By type vs by feature
steps.narration: By type: folders named after what a file is (components/, hooks/, pages/); a feature is scattered across them, and components/ grows into one long list of unrelated files. By feature: folders named after what part of the product a file serves; things that change together sit together, a feature can be read, moved or deleted as a unit, and imports between features are visible. I chose by feature because this app is three views that barely share UI: the Timeline work touches only features/timeline, and nobody has to scan 20 components to find one. By type would make sense with many small, heavily shared primitives (a design system). The cost of by-feature is the judgment call about what is shared, which is why ARCHITECTURE.md states the rule.

steps.title: D10 - Q1 — Why reading the query parameter fits the rule
steps.narration: The rule is "no state beyond what is necessary to render the initial view". steps.title: D1 - Q1 — React handler vs inline onclick / addEventListener
steps.narration: Vanilla inline onclick="fn()" is an HTML attribute string evaluated in global scope (that is why main.ts had to copy functions onto window); the browser calls it with its native Event. addEventListener also hands over the native Event, to a function reference, with the listener attached to that exact element. In React you write onClick={fn} on the JSX element and React calls fn with a SyntheticEvent: a cross-browser wrapper with the same API (target, currentTarget, preventDefault, stopPropagation) and a .nativeEvent field to reach the browser's object. So they are not the same kind of object: one is the DOM Event, the other React's wrapper around it. React does not attach a listener to your button at all: since React 17 it registers one listener per event type on the root container and dispatches to the handler props itself, running them in React's own bubbling order.

steps.title: D1 - Q2 — Is event delegation still needed in React?

In React the handler is a prop of the element: when state changes React re-renders, diffs, keeps the existing DOM nodes and just points them at the new function, so nothing is re-registered by me, and removed cards drop their handlers automatically. Internally React does delegate (one listener per event type on the root), but that is its implementation detail, not something I write. The one thing delegation gave for free that I must handle: the nested star button inside the clickable card needs event.stopPropagation() so one click does not also open the detail.

steps.title: D3 - Q1 — Why mutation sometimes looks fine, and what React compares
steps.narration: React does not look inside state. After setState it compares the new value with the old one using Object.is, i.e. reference identity for arrays and objects; if they are the same it skips the render of that component and treats memo children, useMemo and effect dependencies as unchanged. Mutation 'works' on screen whenever something else triggers a render anyway (another setState, a parent update, a keystroke in another field): the render then reads the already-mutated array, so the screen looks right. It breaks whenever the render is skipped or relied on a reference check: the push example above (no render until something else caused one), the React.memo child that kept showing 2 items, a useMemo/dependency array that never re-runs, and time travel/undo or comparing previous and next state, where the 'previous' array already contains the change. Those bugs depend on timing, which is why they are hard to track: the same code looks correct or broken depending on what else happened to render.

steps.title: D4 - Q2 — Why deriving makes both vanilla bug classes structurally impossible
steps.narration: Stale count: the vanilla Dashboard was drawn into the DOM once (viewRendered flag) from a snapshot of state.bookmarks, so later bookmarking changed the data but nothing told the old DOM to change. Computed in render, the number is a function of the current data: every time React renders the component it calls the function again, so there is no moment where the number on screen was computed from older data than the data on hand. There is also no copy that needs an update call that somebody can forget. Aliased array: filteredEvidence was assigned the same reference as allEvidence, so sorting 'the view' sorted the master. In the derived version there is no variable named 'the filtered list' that can be assigned or aliased; the list is the return value of filter(), which always allocates a new array, and it is thrown away and rebuilt on every render, so even an in-place sort only touches the throwaway. Both bugs need a second stored thing that has to stay equal to a first one; derive and the second thing does not exist. Less likely vs impossible: a stored copy can always be forgotten, a derived value cannot be out of date by construction (as long as the inputs themselves are state or props).

steps.title: D6 - Q1 — Why a nested child should not change distant state itself
steps.narration: React data flows one way, down. A child cannot reach up and set a parent's state: it only has what it was given. It would need the setter (or the storage module) imported or passed, which means (1) the rules for changing that state (immutable update, persistence, error message) get copied into every child that touches it, (2) the owner no longer controls how its state changes, so you cannot know who changed it by reading the owner, and (3) the child is welded to that particular state and cannot be reused or shown with different data. Mutating a parent's object from the child is the worst version: no render is scheduled (Demo 3). A callback prop gives a single named entry point, the owner's function: the child states what happened ('save this note'), the owner decides how state changes. It also keeps the child presentational: EvidenceDetail only gets text and functions and can be rendered with fake ones.

steps.title: D7 - Q1 — Why evidence filters suit useReducer
steps.narration: They are one domain: seven values that are read together (the list is a function of all seven), changed by a small fixed set of events (set one, change sort, clear), and reset together. With useState each of those facts is spread over code: seven declarations, a switch that routes a field to its setter, a clear function that must list every setter, and a toolbar contract that grew with every filter. With useReducer the whole 'what can happen to filters' is one pure function: adding a filter means one field in the type and nothing else, because SET_FILTER and CLEAR_FILTERS work for it already. Easier after the switch: clear (one line), testing/reasoning (call the reducer with a state and an action), and a single readable list of the events. The hypothesis form (Demo 2 Q2) stays a useState object: it has no reset, no rules between fields and a single kind of change, 'field X is now Y', which updateField already expresses; a reducer would add ceremony there without removing any.

steps.title: D7 - Q2 — CLEAR_FILTERS

With individual setters the reset is a list that has to be kept in sync by hand: when sortOrder or a new filter is added, forgetting one setter in handleClearFilters leaves that control set after Clear, and nothing fails to compile or run. With the reducer the reset has no list of fields at all, so a field added later is reset automatically, and because the new state is created from a single value the reset is atomic: React renders once with all fields reset, never with some cleared and some not. steps.title: D7 - Q3 — useState is a special case of useReducer
steps.narration: Same idea, different packaging. Both hold a value across renders, both schedule a re-render when you dispatch/set, and both compare the new state to the old with Object.is. A reducer is (state, action) => nextState; useState is the case where the action IS the next state (or a function of the previous state) and the reducer is just 'return that'. React in fact implements useState with the same machinery as useReducer and a built-in reducer, basicStateReducer. The difference is where the update logic lives: useState puts it at every call site (setX(...)), useReducer puts it in one function you name and can read separately from the components that trigger it. Use useState when updates are 'replace the value'; reach for useReducer when there are several related fields or several kinds of change. Not fundamentally different, and you can rewrite one as the other.

steps.title: D8 - Q1 — What Context solves, and what it does not
steps.narration: Solves: prop drilling. A value provided high in the tree can be read by any descendant with useContext, without every component in between declaring and forwarding a prop. Does NOT: (1) it is not state; the state is still useState/useReducer in the provider, Context just transports the value; (2) it is not a store: no selectors, so every consumer re-renders whenever the provided value changes, even if it only uses one field (here that is fine, a combined notes+bookmarks context would re-render the Dashboard on every note save); (3) no built-in persistence, devtools, middleware or derived/cached values; (4) it only reaches descendants of the provider, so it is not 'global'; (5) it makes data flow implicit: a component's inputs are no longer visible in its props. The expectation that it behaves like Redux/Zustand breaks at (2) and (3): it solves delivery, not state management.

steps.title: D10 - Q2 — Structurally gone: forgetting to re-render a view
steps.narration: Exercise 1's defect: views were drawn into the DOM by hand and guarded by viewRendered flags, so after data changed the screen stayed old until someone remembered to call the right render function (the stale Dashboard bookmark count). In React that category cannot be written: a component is a function from props and state to a description of the UI, React calls it again whenever state it uses changes, and there is no render function to forget and no DOM kept between renders to go stale. steps.title: Exercise 6 — Effects, Data Fetching & a Backend
steps.narration: Section marker: from here on the deck is Exercise 6. Until now every view read its data from static data/*.json files, which can only ever be instant or 404. This exercise first teaches render versus effects, dependency arrays and cleanup, then adds a small read-only Node backend with a simulated delay and error, consumes it from React with loading, error and empty states, fixes request races with AbortController, extracts a reusable hook, separates UI, application logic and API access, and closes with the data-flow picture and a written UX decision.

steps.title: D1 - T1 — On the page: a component that does work while rendering
steps.narration: Before the code: this throwaway sandbox page has a BAD component. Its counter should show 1 after the first render, but it shows 2, and it jumps by 2 every time I click re-render parent. Nothing in the UI looks wrong at a glance, which is exactly why render-time side effects are dangerous.

steps.title: D1 - T1 — Side effects written directly in the render body
steps.narration: The BAD component does three things in its render body: it mutates a module variable (badRenderCounter += 1), it calls console.log, and it reads localStorage inline. It seems to work because the screen shows plausible values, but each one is a side effect: it changes or reads something outside the component, so the result no longer depends only on props and state. Under StrictMode React renders twice on purpose to expose exactly this, and the counter proves it: it goes 2 on mount and +2 per update, not +1. The GOOD version only computes JSX during render; logging runs in an effect after commit and the localStorage read runs in an effect that stores the result in state. Verified with Playwright in the sandbox: counter 2 after mount, 4 after one re-render.

steps.title: D1 - T2 — On the page: the good component
steps.narration: Before the code: the GOOD line below the bad one only changes when I click its own re-render button, and its logging happens in an effect. This is the pattern the rule describes.

steps.title: D1 - T2 — My rule: render vs. effect
steps.narration: Rule in my own words: render describes what the screen should look like for the current props and state, and nothing else. It may read props, state and context and compute new values from them, but it must not change anything outside itself and must give the same output for the same input. Anything that reaches outside React or depends on time, the network, the browser or storage (subscriptions, timers, fetch, document.title, writing to localStorage) belongs in an effect, which runs after the render was committed to the screen, or in an event handler if it is caused by a user action. Why this split: React is free to call render several times, pause it or throw its result away, so only code that is safe to repeat can live there.

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — Why React renders more than once
steps.narration: React treats a component as a pure function of props and state, so it is allowed to call it again whenever it wants: for a state update, a parent re-render, a concurrent render that gets interrupted or discarded, or in development under Strict Mode, where it deliberately renders twice (and runs effects twice) to expose impure code. If render ran twice with my side-effect example, the module counter would be wrong (it counts renders, not visits, and the screen shows 2 after mount instead of 1), the console log would be duplicated, and a render-time write such as appending to a list or sending an analytics call would happen twice. The fix is not to avoid double renders but to make render safe to repeat. Verified: counter 2 after mount, 4 after one update.

That is why the rule says: derive during render, do not store it in state and do not compute it in an effect, because a second copy would have to be kept in sync. The only caveat is that the derivation must not mutate its input (Exercise 5 Demo 3: filter and sort on a copy).

steps.title: D2 - Q1 — What React compares in the dependency array
steps.narration: After every render React compares each entry of the new dependency array with the same position in the previous array using Object.is (shallow identity: primitives by value, objects and arrays by reference). If at least one differs, the effect from the previous render is cleaned up and the new one runs; if none differs it is skipped. So a new object or array literal created in render counts as changed every time, and a mutated object counts as unchanged. If I omit a value the effect uses, the effect keeps the closure of the render where it last ran, so it reads a stale value (for example an old search term or an old id) and does not re-run when that value changes. That is why the lint rule exhaustive-deps exists: list everything the effect reads from the component scope.

steps.title: D7 - Q2 — Cleanup and abort are the same thing here
steps.narration: They are connected, not separate: abort() is what the cleanup function does. React decides when to run the cleanup (before the effect re-runs because [request] changed, on unmount, and in Strict Mode dev); my cleanup, return () => controller.abort(), decides what happens then. abort() makes the browser cancel the request and makes the pending fetch promise reject with an AbortError. That rejection arrives in my error callback, which must not show it as an error, so the callback first checks controller.signal.aborted and returns. So three pieces: effect creates the controller, cleanup aborts it, the callbacks ignore anything from an aborted controller. Without the cleanup nothing would ever abort a superseded request; without the aborted check the abort would flash an error box.

steps.title: D8 - Q1 — Custom hook versus helper function
steps.narration: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks (useState, useEffect, useCallback) inside. That is what makes it different from a helper such as fetchJson: a helper only computes and returns, it has no memory between renders and no lifecycle; a hook gives each calling component its own state and effects, tied to that component's mount, update and unmount. React enforces the Rules of Hooks: call hooks only at the top level of a component or another hook, never in loops, conditions, nested functions or after an early return, and never from ordinary functions, because React identifies each hook by its call order within a render. The use prefix lets lint tooling check these rules; I did call all five useFetch hooks unconditionally and before any return.

steps.title: D10 - T2 — One UX decision and what I would change
steps.narration: Decision: the error state states what failed, why and what to do, and offers a Try again button, instead of a bare "Something went wrong". steps.title: Exercise 7 — WebSockets & Multiuser Applications
steps.narration: Section marker: from here on the deck is Exercise 7. Until now the app only pulled data: every view asked the Node API with fetch() and learned about changes by asking again. This exercise adds one small real-time feature on top: several browser tabs share the bookmarks of one investigation Workspace and see each other's changes without reloading. It compares request-response with WebSockets, builds the minimal connection lifecycle, gives each connection a name and a presence list, defines a small typed message protocol shared by browser and server, keeps the shared bookmark set in server memory behind a small session object, broadcasts every change, handles disconnect and reconnect, validates every incoming message, and closes with the data-flow picture and the honest limitations.

steps.title: D1 - T1 — fetch() vs. WebSocket comparison (page)
steps.narration: Before the code: the Evidence list on screen was delivered by exactly one fetch("api/evidence"): one request, one response. Nothing in this page can change unless the browser asks again. The comparison on the next slide sets that against a WebSocket.

steps.title: D1 - T1 — fetch() vs. WebSocket comparison
steps.narration: Comparison of the Exercise 6 fetch() and a WebSocket along the three required points. Who can send: with fetch only the client starts an exchange and the server answers once; with a WebSocket both sides can send at any time once it is open. How long it lives: a fetch is one request and its response (no conversation state afterwards); a WebSocket lives from the handshake until someone closes it or the network breaks. How the client learns of a server-side change: with fetch only by asking again (reload, retry, polling); with a WebSocket the server pushes a message and the client reacts in its message handler. Why this matters for this exercise: bookmarks can be changed by another tab at any moment, and a pull-only protocol cannot tell this tab. The full table (including cost and failure modes) is in docs/exercise-7/01-http-vs-websocket.md.

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — Why polling is less suitable for live bookmarks (page)

steps.title: D1 - Q1 — Why polling is less suitable for live bookmarks
steps.narration: Polling means asking "anything new?" every N seconds. If N is large, a colleague's bookmark shows up seconds late; if N is small, almost every request answers "nothing changed" yet still costs a full HTTP exchange (headers, routing, a response) per tab per interval, and the server does that work for every idle tab. The bookmark set is tiny and changes rarely and unpredictably, which is the worst case for polling: either slow or wasteful. A WebSocket sends one small frame only when a bookmark actually changes, and it arrives at once. Cost grows with changes, not with time times tabs.

steps.title: D1 - Q2 — Why REST endpoints stay

HTTP gives status codes, caching, AbortController cancellation, the Vite proxy and easy debugging with curl or the Network panel for free. The WebSocket carries only the small, fast-changing shared state (bookmark ids and presence). Also, a bookmark id such as E03 is meaningful only against the evidence delivered by REST, so the socket complements REST instead of replacing it. Moving everything to the socket would throw away caching and tooling and would force me to reinvent request/response matching on top of it.

steps.title: D1 - Q3 — When polling is reasonable
steps.narration: Polling is the right tool when updates are rare or a delay of seconds is acceptable (a build status page, a dashboard refreshing every minute), when the infrastructure cannot hold long-lived connections (some proxies, serverless platforms, corporate firewalls), when there are very few clients, or when simplicity beats latency: polling is stateless on the server and needs no reconnect or presence logic at all. It is also the fallback many libraries use when a WebSocket cannot be established. For live bookmarks it loses, but for "how many items are reviewed" a refresh every 30 seconds would be fine.

steps.title: D1 - Q4 — When Server-Sent Events fit better
steps.narration: Server-Sent Events (EventSource) are a one-way stream from server to client over plain HTTP. They are better when the client only listens (live log, notifications, progress of a long job, price ticker): the browser reconnects automatically, resumes with Last-Event-ID, and it works through ordinary HTTP infrastructure. A WebSocket is better when the client also sends frequently and with low latency, like bookmark toggles here, because SSE would need a separate POST request per toggle. The bookmarks need both directions, so WebSocket is the better fit here; a read-only activity feed would be an SSE case.

Each of open, message, close and error is logged on both sides (browser console prefix [live], server log prefix [realtime]); I checked them in the real browser: open then message with "Server received: Hello from the Workspace"; with the backend stopped, a page load shows error then close with code 1006 and the status disconnected. The cleanup function closes the socket with code 1000 so a connection never outlives its component; because of that StrictMode shows a first connection closed before it was established, and the isCurrent flag stops that stale socket's late close event from overwriting the live status of the second one. The Vite proxy entry for /ws has ws: true so the upgrade is forwarded.

steps.title: D2 - Q1 — Why the handshake is HTTP (page)

steps.title: D2 - Q1 — Why the handshake is HTTP
steps.narration: A WebSocket starts as an ordinary HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket and Connection: Upgrade headers; the server answers 101 Switching Protocols and from then on the same TCP connection carries WebSocket frames. Why: it reuses everything that already exists for HTTP on port 80/443: proxies, firewalls and load balancers let it through, TLS (wss) and cookies/origin checks work, one server port serves both the API and the socket (here /api and /ws on 3001), and a server that does not know WebSockets simply answers an ordinary error. Visible proof in this exercise: a request to /nothing as WebSocket is refused with an HTTP status, and the Vite proxy needs only ws: true to forward the same handshake.

steps.title: D2 - Q2 — Open, closed, failed attempt
steps.narration: Open: the handshake succeeded, readyState is OPEN, the open event fired, both sides can send. Closed: it was open (or closing) and ended, the close event fires with a code, a reason and wasClean (1000 normal, 1001 going away, 1006 abnormal with no close frame). Failed connection attempt: the handshake never completed, so there was never an open event; the browser fires error and then close with code 1006 and the reason stays empty (it deliberately gives no detail for security reasons). I saw both: backend stopped before loading the page gave error then close 1006 without any open; stopping the backend while the tab was live gave close 1006 after open and message. So the way to tell them apart in code is whether open ever fired.

steps.title: D3 - Q3 — When presence is temporarily wrong
steps.narration: A tab crash, a killed browser, a laptop losing power or a cable pull sends no close frame, and the server only learns the connection is dead when TCP gives up (it can take minutes) or a write fails. Until then the dead user stays in the list as a ghost. The opposite error also exists: a user with a flaky network is still listed although they cannot receive anything. The usual fix is a heartbeat: the server pings every few seconds and terminates connections that did not answer with a pong, which turns a ghost into a removal within seconds (named as an extension in the exercise, not built here).

steps.title: D4 - Q1 — Why a type discriminator
steps.narration: With one object with many optional properties (name?, names?, bookmarks?, evidenceId?) the compiler cannot say which fields exist: every access needs a check, impossible combinations are allowed (a welcome that carries bookmarks, a toggle without an evidenceId), and a typo goes unnoticed. With a discriminated union, checking message.type narrows the object: inside case "presence-updated" TypeScript knows names exists and is a string[], and inside case "welcome" it knows name does. The type is also the natural switch key, and a switch with an assertNever default makes forgetting a case a compile error. It is clearer for readers, too: the union is the complete list of what can be said.

steps.title: D4 - Q2 — How the types are shared

Vite and Node (type stripping) erase the types, so no runtime code is shared or bundled. The problem it prevents is drift: I tested it by renaming names to users in the protocol only, and tsc immediately failed on both sides: react/shared/live/useWorkspaceSocket.ts(55,36): error TS2339: Property 'names' does not exist on type '{ type: 'presence-updated'; users: string[]; }'. | server/realtime.ts(31,7): error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'names' does not exist in type '{ type: 'presence-updated'; users: string[]; }'.. Without a shared file each side would keep its own idea of the shape, and the mismatch would show up only at runtime as an undefined value in the UI.

steps.title: D5 - Q1 — Why the server is the source of truth

steps.title: D6 - Q2 — Why broadcast the complete set

A sequence of operations (E14 added, E03 removed, ...) would require every client to apply them in the same order exactly once, to track which operation it saw last, and to ask for the missed ones after a disconnect: much more machinery for no benefit at this size.

steps.title: D6 - Q3 — Sender gets its own broadcast, or optimistic?

steps.title: D7 - Q4 — A version number to detect stale writes
steps.narration: Keep a counter in WorkspaceSession and increase it on every change; send it with every state message (version: 12). The client remembers the last version it saw and sends it with its write ({ type: "toggle-bookmark", evidenceId, baseVersion: 12 }). If baseVersion is older than the server's current version, the write was made against stale state: the server rejects it (or applies it and flags it) and answers with the current state so the client can warn the user. The same counter also lets a client notice that it missed a message (a gap in versions) and ask for request-state.

steps.title: D8 - Q3 — What a heartbeat detects that close and error may not
steps.narration: A half-open connection: the other end vanished without a close frame (Wi-Fi dropped, laptop slept, a NAT or proxy silently discarded the idle connection, the server host froze). TCP can take minutes to notice, so the browser fires neither close nor error and the badge still says Live while nothing arrives and sent messages disappear. A heartbeat (ping every N seconds, expect a pong within a few seconds) turns silence into a detectable event: no pong means treat the connection as dead, close it and reconnect. steps.title: D9 - Q3 — How a client could impersonate a display name

An attacker can therefore open and close connections until the server hands out the name it wants (the other holder must have left; two live connections never share a name), and a user who reconnects can end up with someone else's former name. If the app ever added a "rename" message, nothing would stop a client from picking another person's name, because the server would have only the unauthenticated claim to go on. Real identity needs authentication (a signed-in session or token checked during the handshake) and the server attaching the authenticated user to the connection.

steps.narration: One session shared by everyone; state in memory only (a restart empties it); one server process; no authentication or authorization (display names are random labels, not identities); no Origin check and no rate limit (only a 16 KiB frame limit); plain ws://; no heartbeat (a silently dead connection is noticed late, so presence can have ghosts and the Live badge can be wrong for a while); one automatic reconnect without backoff; no offline editing (stars are disabled instead of queueing); a toggle, not an idempotent set, so simultaneous toggles of one item cancel out; only bookmarks are live (notes, review edits and the hypothesis stay local); dev only, not part of the GitHub Pages deploy; and the React components are checked by hand in a real browser, there is no browser test runner. steps.after:
## Limitations of this exercise

- **One session.** Every connection shares one bookmark set; there are no rooms or cases.
- **In-memory only.** A server restart empties the bookmarks; names and presence are rebuilt.
- **One server process.** A second instance would have its own set and its own tabs.
- **No authentication or authorization.** Anyone who can reach the port can connect, see everyone,
  and toggle any bookmark. Display names are random labels, not identities, and are reused.
- **No Origin check and no rate limit.** Another website could open the socket from a visitor's
  browser; a valid message can be repeated without limit (the frame size is limited to 16 KiB).
- **Plain `ws://`** in development; production needs `wss://`.
- **No heartbeat.** A silently dead connection is noticed late, so presence can show ghosts and
  the Live badge can be wrong for a while.
- **One automatic reconnect, no backoff.** After that the user presses Reconnect.
- **No offline editing.** While disconnected the stars are disabled instead of queueing changes.
- **Toggle, not set.** Two users toggling the same item at once cancel each other out.
- **Only bookmarks are live.** Notes, review edits and the hypothesis are still local to the tab.
- **Dev only.** Like the Exercise 6 API, the WebSocket server is not part of the GitHub Pages
  deploy, so there the React page shows the disconnected state and cannot change bookmarks.
  The vanilla `index.html` app is unchanged and keeps its own local bookmarks.
- **Tests.** The server and the reconnect logic have automated tests; the React components are
  checked in a real browser by hand (there is no browser test runner in this project).

steps.title: D10 - Q1 — If one step silently stopped
steps.narration: I pick the broadcast. If server-side session.broadcast silently did nothing, the server would still validate and store the toggle, nobody would see an error, and no tab would ever change: not even the one that clicked, because the sender also waits for the broadcast. What breaks: the whole point, sharing, but quietly; the app looks alive (Live badge, stars enabled). How I would notice: the server log shows "message ... toggle-bookmark" while the browser console shows no "[live] message ... bookmarks-updated"; a reload makes the correct set appear, because a new connection is sent the state, which is the tell that only the fan-out is broken; the integration test (toggle from one real client reaches both) fails; and the stale tab is repaired by the next request-state. steps.title: Opt - Q1 — Live notes with an editing indicator, without a merge algorithm
steps.narration: When someone opens a note they send { type: "note-editing", evidenceId } and when they stop (or their connection closes) { type: "note-idle", evidenceId }. The server keeps a map evidenceId -> editor name, exactly like presence, and broadcasts it, so every tab can show "Investigator-42 is editing" next to the note and the others can wait, or be asked to confirm before editing too. Saving is an explicit action that sends the whole note text; the server stores it and broadcasts it. There is no merge because a person is expected to edit alone at a time (a soft lock: a hint, not enforcement). The editor entry must be removed on close, and ideally expire after inactivity, or a crashed tab blocks the note forever (the ghost problem of Demo 3).

steps.narration: Before the code: optional extension question; the live part of this page is the starting point.

steps.title: Opt - Q2 — Last-write-wins with a warning for notes, and why not for a long document
steps.narration: Every note carries a version. The editor sends { evidenceId, text, baseVersion }. The server always applies the newest write and increases the version; if baseVersion was older than the current version the write overwrote someone else's change, so the server tells the sender ("you replaced a newer version by Investigator-44") and tells the overwritten author their version was replaced. Nobody is blocked and the code is small. For a short note that is acceptable: the loss is a sentence, and the warning lets people restore it. For a long document it is unsuitable: edits last minutes, so collisions are likely; one overwrite throws away a large amount of work that is hard to spot and merge by eye; two people editing different paragraphs would still destroy each other's changes. That needs per-section locks or a real merge (operational transformation, CRDT).

steps.title: Opt - Q3 — Optimistic UI that still reconciles with the server
steps.narration: Show the change immediately and keep it as pending: the client gives each action an id, adds it to a list of pending actions, renders (server state + pending actions), and sends it with the id. When the server answers, the pending action with that id is removed and the display is again just the server's state, which now includes the change, or, if the server refused it (error), the action is dropped, the star flips back and the reason is shown. If the connection is lost with actions pending, they are either dropped with a visible notice or resent after request-state, which works only if the operation is idempotent (set-bookmark, not toggle). The server's state always wins; the optimistic layer only covers the round trip. I did not do it here because the round trip is milliseconds and it would add this machinery for no visible gain.

steps.title: Opt - Q4 — Duplicate or stale messages across reconnects although TCP preserves order
steps.narration: TCP guarantees order and delivery only inside one connection. A reconnect is a new connection, a new ordering domain: (1) messages the server broadcast during the outage are never delivered, so the client is stale until it asks for the state; (2) a client that sent a toggle just before the drop does not know whether it arrived; if it resends, the server may apply it twice (a toggle is not idempotent), and if it does not, the change may be lost; (3) late events from the old socket can arrive after the new one is open (the isCurrent guard in ReconnectingSocket exists for that); (4) with several tabs or servers there is no single order across connections at all. The defences: send the complete state on (re)connect, make operations idempotent, give messages ids or version numbers so duplicates and gaps are detectable, and ignore events from superseded sockets.
